In this installment, Barbie is a smart coder who designs, programs and tests a video game with her friends, and who patiently includes her younger sister and encourages her to try coding too. When the game's in-game tutorial asks her to help with a beta test, Barbie hesitates for only a moment before clicking "yes", and she is magically pulled into the world of her favorite game, where she is delighted to find herself transformed into a fun roller-skating character. Inside the game she meets Cutie, a lovable cloud-shaped companion, and Bella, the roller-skating princess, along with another character, Kris. It soon emerges that the real reason Barbie has been invited in is that a mischievous emoji, a computer virus, is trying to take control of the game and destroy everything in it, and the only way to defeat it is to win every level. The in-game characters, who are used to doing things a certain way, are not always ready to cooperate, so Barbie must rely on her gaming skills, her coding knowledge and her out-of-the-box thinking, as well as on teamwork, to save her new friends and beat the game. As the group travels through three colorful levels, each introducing new characters, a growing horde of viruses causes more and more mayhem.

The film was released on DVD and digital platforms at the end of January 2017, with Barbie Dreamtopia shorts as bonus material. Common Sense Media's Andrea Beach rated it suitable for ages five and up and called it a gentle, fun adventure that Barbie fans would enjoy, praising its portrayal of Barbie as a coder who thinks problems through, its simple explanations of code, computer viruses and non-player characters, and its messages about teamwork, perseverance and creative problem-solving, which she felt could encourage girls to explore programming. The review regretted, however, that the film never addresses online safety after Barbie clicks to accept an unknown invitation.

Patterson plays Maggie Marks, a young American lawyer who, at her father's urging, is about to begin her first job at a large New York law firm. Before starting, she takes a last-minute winter holiday with her best friend, Sarah Price (Rhea Bailey), to the small European kingdom of Calpurnia. There she meets a charming and daring young man and agrees to a date, unaware that he is Prince Adrian (Donnelly), the heir to the throne, who is about to be crowned king. His mother, Queen Beatrice (Bond), disapproves of his carefree lifestyle and his habit of slipping out of the palace to enjoy himself rather than preparing for his future duties. Maggie and Adrian quickly feel a kinship, since each is facing a "job" neither really wants.

When Maggie discovers Adrian's true identity and reads press reports portraying him as a playboy, she confronts him, and he invites her to keep spending time with him so that she can judge him for herself. At a palace dinner she feels out of place and understands why he so often escapes. Photographs of the couple soon appear in the press, displeasing both Maggie's father, who fears the publicity will harm a future lawyer, and the queen, who uses her influence with Maggie's future employer to lure her back to New York. Torn between a secure career and her young romance with a future monarch, Maggie resolves to cut short her holiday, regretting that she will miss his coronation, which, contrary to tradition, is to be held in public. In the end the queen apologises, having changed her mind about Maggie, and gives the couple her blessing; Maggie attends the coronation and extends her stay in King Adrian's realm indefinitely.

German critics found the film conventional but pleasant. TV Spielfilm called it the usual holiday love story but quite charming, while the Lexikon des internationalen Films noted its attractive settings and familiar, easily resolved complications, judging it comparatively acceptable thanks to solid performances and a light tone.

Diana Prieto (Ramírez), a well-off housewife in Santiago, is pregnant with her second child while struggling to care for her first, Martin (Bassi), a boy of about ten with severe autism who can be unpredictably violent and must be restrained at night so he does not hurt himself. Her husband Tomás (Tapia Montt) is often away on business trips to Japan, and every nanny they hire quits within days. When Martin has a violent outburst in a supermarket, a Filipina employee, Luz (Jabolin), calms him almost instantly. Diana hires her, and Luz explains that her own son David (Durán) was once like Martin and is now cured. Under her care Martin improves dramatically, but Diana grows uneasy: Luz speaks to the boy only in her own language, takes him off his medication without permission, and strange homemade charms begin turning up around the house. Using an instant translation app, Diana becomes convinced that Luz is turning her son against her through voodoo, and as she suffers nausea, rashes and hallucinations, she begins to fear that the nanny is poisoning her too, in a game that may prove deadly.

In 2013, Miriam, a high-achieving student who campaigns on behalf of victims of abuse, is admitted to Duke, but without financial aid. Her father promises to pay her tuition, but after she moves into her dormitory he leaves for work in Afghanistan, and her mother tells her the family cannot afford the fees and suggests a student loan. Desperate, Miriam half-jokingly considers adult films, applies online as Belle Knox, and accepts a shoot in New York, afterwards crying in a bathroom. She then signs with an agent, Don (Nelson), who books her work in Los Angeles. Lying to her family about where the tuition money comes from, she keeps her double life secret until a classmate, Jeff, recognises her, swears to keep quiet and then spreads the news anonymously online.

As rumours spread, Miriam faces vicious online attacks and unwanted attention. She fights back by giving an interview to the student newspaper's reporter Amanda (Lu), describing her work as empowering and feminist, but the published piece distorts her words, and once Belle Knox's identity becomes public she is condemned by many. She tells her conservative family, meeting her mother's condemnation and her father's rejection, appears live on CNN, and later finds her parents ready to accept her, though her brother disowns her. At an adult film awards ceremony in Las Vegas she is shunned by colleagues over her outspoken interviews. The film ends in January 2015, with Miriam giving a motivational speech on women's rights and freedom of choice and telling Amanda that she plans to go into politics.

Reviews were mixed. Lifetime Uncorked gave it four out of five, and The Solute recommended it despite plot holes and an unclear heroine, while The Best Darn Girls gave it three out of five, finding its message muddled. AVN's Peter Warren criticised it as ill-informed about the adult industry and more fiction than biography.

An enormous ancient artifact is unearthed in a desert quarry. When its discoverer, Brian Carter (Newman), is murdered by Nicole (Kincer), the henchwoman of Kontral, an agent of a shadowy cabal, Kontral hires the researcher Daniel Allen and his assistant and lover Scout to translate the inscriptions on it, which reveal a 14,000-year-old love letter from a woman to her god. The object proves to be a spacecraft left behind by an advanced human civilization that predates recorded history, and it still appears to be functional. Once their work is done, the cabal tries to eliminate them; Daniel is killed and Scout, framed for his death, goes on the run, troubled by visions of an unknown woman who seems to be guiding her. Captured, she turns out to have a mysterious connection with the craft, and her presence awakens a red robot, which takes her and Kontral aboard and flies them to the Moon. There a blue robot attacks; Kontral tries to escape in the ship, and the two machines fight until the red one is destroyed. Using a stone it carried, Scout activates an ancient temple that gives the Moon a breathable atmosphere. Inside she finds Garen, the god of the Krell people, in stasis, and learns from Mya, the woman of her visions, that she has been chosen to fulfill Mya's failed destiny. Scout joins Garen in suspended animation, and the first plants sprout on the lunar surface.

Sony released the film on DVD in the United States in early 2017, and Gilt Edge Media issued it in the United Kingdom. Reviews were negative. Phil Wheat of Nerdly, a fan of the original, found it structurally confusing, like a fevered dream, and slow to reach the Moon, though he welcomed the return of the robots and its grotesque finale. Mana Pop called the script incoherent and the effects among the cheapest it had seen, and the German Lexikon des internationalen Films judged that it failed through both lack of competence and lack of money.

The story is deliberately simple. Walter Cooke (Jacobus) is a blind man and an apple pie connoisseur who needs milk to go with his latest pie, so he heads to his neighbourhood corner store to buy milk and fresh apples. While he is shopping, his friend the shopkeeper, Gordon (Yuan), is confronted by a group of mafia thugs who are shaking him down for money he owes them. The gangsters underestimate the quiet customer, and Walter springs into action, single-handedly taking on the three men and showing them what a blind martial artist is capable of.

The film consists essentially of one extended fight scene. In its early stages Jacobus plays much of the action for comedy, using his cane as a prop in the manner of some of Jackie Chan's best fights, before it escalates into a fast and technically demanding weapons battle of parries, blocks and strikes. Barber's fluid camerawork keeps the geography of the fight clear throughout. During the end credits, footage shows Jacobus training blindfolded to learn how to portray a man without sight convincingly.

The short was warmly received by martial arts and action critics. The Action Elite awarded it full marks, calling it massively entertaining, one of the best short films its reviewer had seen in years, and further proof that Jacobus deserved bigger films, while hoping that Walter would return in a feature. Michael S. Moore of Kiai-Kick gave it 9.5 out of 10 and called it Jacobus's best film yet, praising Barber's direction, Yuan's choreography, the production values and the way the cast packed so much character into a brief running time, his only complaint being that he wanted more.

Max is assigned to the White House to fill in while the resident Secret Service dog is on maternity leave, and he quickly bonds with T.J., the president's twelve-year-old son, who is struggling to lead a normal life in the bubble created by his father's position. When the Russian president arrives for negotiations on a nuclear arms treaty, bringing his daughter Alex, T.J. is asked to keep her company. The two become friends, and when they sneak out of the White House in search of a party thrown by T.J.'s new classmates, masked men try to kidnap them. Max, who has followed them, fends off the attackers, and the children escape into trouble with their parents.

Convinced that someone wants the talks to fail, T.J. and Alex start investigating everyone they suspect, but their sleuthing keeps backfiring. After further danger, including an attempt to harm the First Lady that Max narrowly foils, the Secret Service persuades the president to take Max off duty, and the angry Russian leader prepares to cut his visit short. Unable to sleep, T.J. discovers that Coop, the White House chef, is a Russian mole, and is locked in a freezer while Olga lures Alex into the woods to be abducted. Max breaks out of his cage to free T.J., and a chase involving both presidents and Agent Thorn ends with the culprits captured and Alex rescued. The fathers resume their talks and reach a historic agreement, Max is honoured for bravery, and the resident dog's three puppies await T.J.

Filmed in and around Vancouver, British Columbia, in June and July 2016, the film was released in May 2017 and came to DVD and Blu-ray from Warner Bros. Home Entertainment on May 23. Common Sense Media called it a conventional, harmless and forgettable story kept moving by its engaging young leads and the dog's exploits, and Forbes concluded that it was simply meant for kids, who could do better but also much worse.

Butler plays Laura Halpern, a restless, overprotective mother whose marriage of ten years to Greg (Benson) has lost its spark; with her husband away at work and her young son Jamie at school, she dreams of renovating her kitchen to fill her days. The family keeps a boat at a dock near Elliott Graverston (Rosner), a handsome contractor who rescues Jamie when the boy falls into the water. Invited to dinner, Elliott offers to remodel the kitchen and is soon working in the house, shirtless, under the admiring eyes of Laura and her neighbour Mira (Frigon). When Laura finds a pair of women's underwear on the boat and concludes that Greg is cheating, Elliott confides that as a child he had to help his mother cope with unfaithful men, and the two begin a passionate affair.

Racked with guilt, Laura tries to end it, but Elliott refuses to let her go, and she later learns that Greg's supposed lover, his assistant, was merely planning a surprise party for him. When the assistant goes home with Elliott and finds Laura's photograph by his bed, he strangles her. Elliott starts leaving notes in Laura's house and threatens to reveal the affair, and Laura discovers through a former client, a woman who resembles her, and a local café owner that he has a history of obsession, a possessive attachment to his mother and suspected involvement in a fire that destroyed his family home. Elliott kidnaps Greg and holds him on his boat, then takes Laura and Jamie captive at home in a twisted "anniversary" dinner. Laura knocks him down with a wine bottle but is struck with a hammer and carried to the boat, where she frees herself, stabs Elliott, rescues Greg and finally sends her pursuer falling to his death from a high window.

Patrick Serrano of the review site Lifetime Uncorked, recapping it with tongue firmly in cheek, gave it a rating of four knives for its thrills, along with a recommendation of three glasses of wine.

The short opens with little Dennis begging his parents, Mavis and Johnny, for a puppy. Mavis gently refuses, explaining that a pet is a big responsibility, and when Johnny suggests a goldfish instead, the heartbroken boy turns into a bat and flies off wailing that he wants a puppy. Dracula finds his grandson sulking on a window ledge and, unable to resist the boy's pleading face, agrees to get him one. Soon a knock at the door is followed by an enormous blue dog bursting into the family's living room, flattening Dracula against a wall. Dennis is overjoyed and names his new friend Tinkles, while Mavis glares at her father, who insists that every monster needs a good pet, and then discovers that the giant puppy has already had an accident on her floor.

The next night, Mavis asks a sleepy Dracula to look after Tinkles while she takes Dennis to school. The count barely gets back into his coffin before the dog wakes him needing to go outside, then demands to be fed. Dracula brings a wheelbarrow of meat and puts the animal through a series of tricks, which goes well until he commands Tinkles to speak and the dog replies, "Hi. How are you?" Back at the front desk, Dracula grows ever more exasperated by the huge pet looming behind him, and when a family of skeletons checks in, Tinkles lunges at them and starts chewing their bones, wrecking the lobby. Returning with Dennis, Mavis is horrified by the chaos and asks what happened; Dracula simply points to the dog, and the short ends with him sighing to the audience that he needs a vacation, a nod to the next film, also hinted at by the cruise brochure Mavis reads.

The voice cast reunites Adam Sandler as Dracula, Selena Gomez as Mavis, Andy Samberg as Johnny and Asher Blinkoff as Dennis, with Joe Whyte as the voice of Tinkles and Rose Abdoo as the hotel's witch maids.

A prologue set during the early years of Augusto Pinochet's military dictatorship shows a boy being indoctrinated and forced by his father to take part in the torture and abuse of the regime's victims. Decades later, four young women, Andrea (Catalina Martin), her sister Camila (Macarena Carrere), Julia (Ximena del Solar) and Magdalena (Dominga Bofill), travel to a remote rural village for a few days away. What first seems like paradise becomes a nightmare when they are brutally attacked and sexually assaulted by Juan (Daniel Antivilo) and his son Mario (Felipe Ríos). Juan is the boy from the prologue, who still believes the principles of the regime must live on, has been terrorising the locals for years, and is raising his son to follow in his footsteps. Finding no help in the town, the survivors join forces with a pair of police officers to confront their attackers, and their resolve hardens when Juan seizes a local girl, leading to a violent final showdown during which Juan sings an old military song.

The film provoked controversy for its scenes of torture, rape, incest, necrophilia and infanticide, and for its condemnation of the Pinochet regime and the way its brutality is handed down from fathers to sons. Rojas and the cast explained that the four leads insisted he show the violence without restraint so that the message would come through; the assault scene took three days to film.

Screen Anarchy's review of the premiere called it one of the most brutal, graphic and disturbing horror films in recent memory, comparable to A Serbian Film but more overt in its political message, praising the four actresses and singling out Antivilo's portrayal of Juan as one of the most terrible villains of the year, while finding the final act's arming of the protagonists somewhat silly.

Zoo is a 2017 Irish-British historical family drama written and directed by Colin McIvor, a Belfast native making his third feature. Loosely based on the true story of Denise Austin, the Belfast woman remembered as the zoo's "elephant angel", it stars Penelope Wilton as Denise Austin, Art Parkinson as Tom Hall, Toby Jones as the security guard Charlie, Emily Flain as Jane, Ian O'Reilly as Pete, James Stockdale as Pete's brother Mickey, Stephen Hagan as the veterinarian Jake, Damian O'Hare and Amy Huberman as Tom's parents, and Ian McElhinney.

In 1941, twelve-year-old Tom dreams of following his father George, who works at the slightly shabby Bellevue Zoo in Belfast, into a life with animals. The highlight of the year is the arrival of a young Asian elephant, whom Tom names Buster. Soon afterwards George is called up to serve in the British Army, leaving Tom and his mother to cope as the war closes in. Worried about Buster, Tom keeps sneaking past the grumpy guard Charlie, only to find the elephant in the care of the hostile Jake.

When German bombers strike the city in the Belfast Blitz, the authorities order the destruction of the zoo's potentially dangerous animals in case they escape during another raid. Realizing that Buster could be next, Tom devises an audacious plan to rescue him. He recruits Jane, a neglected classmate with an alcoholic father, Pete, a former bully who proves softer than he seems, and Pete's brother Mickey, a boy with a disability whose family has kept him hidden from view. Their unlikely ally is Mrs. Austin, a reclusive, eccentric woman who shares her cluttered home with a menagerie of animals and gradually reveals the losses she suffered in an earlier war. Together they spirit the elephant out of the zoo and hide him in her back yard, trying to keep him secret amid the air raids, in what Tom calls the most unforgettable year of his life.

Kylie, a talented baker working as a temporary receptionist for her boyfriend, the real estate developer Alex Hawkey, learns that she has finally become a semifinalist in the American Gingerbread Competition, whose $25,000 prize could help her open a bakery of her own. Expecting a marriage proposal at their anniversary dinner at a local pizzeria, she is instead offered a promotion to office manager, and realizing that Alex does not support her dreams, she breaks up with him. The pizzeria turns out to belong to Nick, her old boyfriend, whom she has not seen in years; he gave up his ambition of becoming a pastry chef to run the family restaurant and is raising Bobby on his own. When Kylie's oven breaks down, Nick lets her use his industrial pizza oven at night, and as she bakes, helps Bobby make cupcakes for a school party and reminisces with Nick about their youthful dreams, their romance is rekindled. Alex, meanwhile, tries to win her back by sponsoring the celebrated "Godmother of Gingerbread", Ina Bruckner, to compete in the same contest. When he stages a grand gesture at the competition, presenting a gingerbread jewelry store containing an engagement ring, Nick assumes Kylie has accepted and pulls away. Realizing she has lost her creative spark trying to imitate Ina, Kylie spends a twelve-hour marathon building a new entry, a moving gingerbread carousel commemorating her first kiss with Nick, wins the prize and reconciles with him at their old carousel.

The film premiered on Hallmark Channel on 11 November 2017. Matt Mueller of OnMilwaukee found it merely "fine", calling Chabert pleasant but given little to work with, Coco nice but bland and Edwards almost too dopey as the ex-boyfriend, while singling out Adams as the most enjoyable character; he likened the film to a Chips Ahoy cookie, sweet enough but not particularly good.

In the year 2138, after twelve years of operation, the immersive online role-playing game Yggdrasil is shutting down its servers. The once-feared guild Ainz Ooal Gown, which had 41 members, has dwindled to almost nothing, and its leader Momonga, a skeletal undead spellcaster, decides to stay in the guild's base, the Great Tomb of Nazarick, until the end. When the deadline passes he finds himself unable to log out, trapped in the body of his avatar, while the non-player characters have gained minds and wills of their own and pledge him absolute loyalty. Realising he is no longer in the game but in a strange new world, Momonga adopts a regal manner and wonders whether his friends were transported too.

When knights attack the nearby Carne Village, he intervenes, saving two young girls and dispatching the attackers with a summoned Death Knight, then rescues the kingdom's Warrior Captain, Gazef Stronoff, from the assassins of the Sunlight Scripture. Taking the guild's name, Ainz Ooal Gown, so that it might become legendary and reach any lost comrades, he unknowingly sets his followers on a path of world conquest. Disguised as the adventurer Momon, he travels to the city of E-Rantel with his battle maid Narberal Gamma, now called Nabe, joins the adventurer team Swords of Darkness to escort the young pharmacist Nfirea Bareare, and tames the legendary Wise King of the Forest, a giant hamster he names Hamsuke, while a cult and the killer Clementine plot to seize Nfirea.

When the virtual reality game Yggdrasil shut down, the guild master Momonga found himself transported with his guild's stronghold, the Great Tomb of Nazarick, and its loyal servants into a real fantasy world, where he took the name Ainz Ooal Gown. Seeking to learn about this world, he poses as the adventurer Momon, accompanied by the battle maid Narberal disguised as Nabe, and joins the adventurers' guild of E-Rantel. Escorting the young Nfirea with the adventurer party Swords of Darkness, Momon tames the legendary Wise King of the Forest, a giant hamster he names Hamsuke. Back in the city, the assassin Clementine and the necromancer Khajiit kidnap Nfirea, slaughter the Swords of Darkness and raise an undead army in the cemetery. Hired by Nfirea's grandmother, Momon tracks them down; Nabe destroys Khajiit and his skeletal dragons, while Momon toys with Clementine before revealing his undead form and crushing her. Meanwhile Shalltear, hunting for martial arts users, falls under the control of a powerful World Class Item wielded by unknown attackers. Realizing that no ordinary means can free her, Ainz decides to face one of Nazarick's strongest guardians himself, defeating her with a meticulously prepared plan built on knowledge from her creator before resurrecting her at great cost. Momon and Nabe are then promoted directly to adamantite rank, becoming the kingdom's third adamantite party.

The Dark Hero opened in Japanese theaters on 11 March 2017, two weeks after The Undead King. The theme song of the two films, "Crazy Scary Holy Fantasy," was performed by Myth & Roid. A second television season was announced during screenings of the second compilation film and premiered in January 2018.

The story is set in Meadowcrest, Kentucky, after the disappearance of a high-school student, Charlie Rice (Hunter Trammell). Local legend holds that an old abandoned mansion is cursed by a witch. Dismissing the stories, Lana (Bader) decides to throw a Halloween party there, and on Halloween night a group of her classmates, among them Shane (Mann), a tough kid who would rather become a mechanic than take career advice from his stepfather, Rachel (Randolph), Dax (Stewart), Brody (Pepe) and Taylor (Belle), slip into the house for a prank, some mischief and a bit of romance. Once inside, the teenagers find themselves trapped. Strange things begin to happen: something drips from the walls, a chair moves on its own, a ghostly woman appears in a mirror and a stew is found simmering in a house that is supposed to be empty. The house turns out to be the domain of a demonic witch who unleashes her wrath on the intruders, and the friends must uncover the secrets hidden in the mansion before they are picked off one by one in increasingly gruesome ways.

The production was filmed in May 2017 at an abandoned mansion on Winchester Road in Lexington, Kentucky; producer Bryan Sexton said the team had looked at some thirty locations before settling on the house, which he considered perfect for a haunted mansion.

Reviews were modest. Dread Central found the film entertaining even though it follows the familiar formula of teenagers ignoring warnings to stay away from a scary house, and Rich Copley of Kentucky Entertainment called the Lexington mansion a prime location for a stylish story. Roger Moore of Movie Nation judged it perfectly watchable in an empty-calories way, singling out the swirling, smoke-like spectre of the house and the on-location footage, but criticised its lack of suspense, generic characters and death scenes borrowed from films such as The Ring and Mama.

At the age of seven, Emma was accused of murdering her mother and her sister, and she has spent the following ten years locked up in Homewood Hall, a gloomy mental institution run by Dr. Patrick Fenton. She insists that the killings were committed by the Stickman, a demonic, black-clawed creature that appears when a certain poem naming him is recited aloud, and that the only way to keep him at bay is to draw a picture of him every night. Her doctors dismiss her account as a delusion. The film opens with one of her nightmares, a bloody attack on a school bus, before revealing her life in the hospital, where her fellow patients include Jeremy, who has not spoken in the six years since he too was accused of killing his parents and who obsessively draws sinister stick figures. A year later, having made enough progress to be released, Emma is placed in a halfway house with five other troubled young women, among them an arsonist and a girl obsessed with the dark web, while Jeremy remains behind. The hostile Liv refuses to believe in the Stickman and does not want to live with a murderer. When the poem is read once again, Emma's nightmares return, and this time the creature crosses into the waking world and begins killing the residents. Convinced that the answer lies at the hospital, Emma tries to find a way to stop it, while Liv remains sure that Emma herself is responsible, until the housemates are forced to band together to survive.

Stickman premiered on Syfy on 21 October 2017 as part of the channel's 31 Days of Halloween programming. Lisa Marie Bowman of Through the Shattered Lens enjoyed it, praising Wilson's ominous atmosphere, shadows and jump scares and calling the creature genuinely creepy. Andy Barkworth of HorrorNews.net found the first half entertaining and nicely shot in a chilly blue palette, but felt the tension evaporated once the unconvincing computer-generated monster was fully shown, and criticized its arbitrary rules and predictability.

Emory (Regan), a newly single travel writer had planned to spend a quiet Christmas alone at home. At short notice, however, her editor hands her an assignment that seems to suit her perfectly: a piece about Christmas in the mountains. She rents a snowbound cabin at a resort in Pine Grove, only to discover on arrival that a reservation mix-up has double-booked it. The other party is Scott Hays (Van Winkle), a widowed lawyer who has reserved the same cabin for himself, his mother Marilyn (Rothery) and his precocious young daughter Katy (Stewart).

With no other cabin available and feeling she cannot argue against a single father, Emory decides to drive back to San Francisco, but a snowstorm sets in and her car will not start in the cold. Scott relents and lets her stay in the fairly roomy cabin. Katy is fascinated by Emory's travel stories. The girl's Christmas wish list, from cutting down their own tree and baking cookies to ice skating and building a snowman, proves a gift to Emory, who can weave the activities into her story. When Marilyn arrives she takes an instant liking to Emory, hoping that her son will open up again after his wife's death. At first the relationship between Scott and Emory remains coolly matter-of-fact, but it warms the more time they spend together. Still, both hesitate to admit their feelings, and Emory leaves without much of a goodbye. When she changes her mind and tries to turn back, her car breaks down again; Scott learns of it and sets out to find her. The two finally talk things through and confess their love, making it the best Christmas ever for all three.

German critics treated the film as a typical example of its genre. TV Spielfilm called it Hallmark television as one knows it, as sugary and sticky as a marshmallow, while Filmdienst described it as a harmless, likeable holiday romance that barely bothers with complications, consisting mostly of a succession of sweet Christmas impressions and stressing the unifying character of the holiday.

The boy DimDimych, a friend of the Fixies, watches his father, a television host, present a show arguing that little people really exist. At the laboratory of the eccentric inventor Professor Chudakov, his assistant Lizonka believes every word of the program, and when the mischievous young Fixie Fire plays tricks on her, she becomes determined to prove the creatures are real and get rid of them. Chudakov then unveils a new invention: energy bracelets that let the Fixies travel through electrical wires into people's homes to carry out "remote repairs", a service he hopes will fund a new laboratory.

Through the professor's carelessness, the bracelets end up with Fire, who is gradually warped by the electricity into a menace, racing through the wires, nearly killing his classmate Verta and finally losing his mind and wrecking DimDimych's family apartment. While the Fixies Simka and Nolik and the elder Fixie Dedus try to catch him, Lizonka summons DimDimych's father to film the little people. DimDimych rushes to the lab to warn his friends, followed by his classmate Katya, who suspects he is hiding a secret, and the humans end up locked in a storeroom when Fire starts a fire. Nolik finds the key, cuts the power to trap Fire inside a socket and saves the day, while the Fixies avoid discovery by turning into tiny screws. Back home, DimDimych and Katya distract the adults by announcing they want to get married while Fire erases the incriminating video, and the cured Fire rejoins his friends as broken equipment around the city begins mysteriously repairing itself.

The film premiered on 27 October 2017 at the Oktyabr cinema in Moscow, opening the Big Cartoon Festival, and was released the following day. Critics called it a worthy feature debut for the studio and praised its colorful graphics, characters and ironic humor, though one regretted that it lacked the educational content of the series. A sequel, The Fixies vs. the Crabots, followed in 2019.

Told through the sessions of a professional dancer, Odette Le Nadant (Bescond), with her psychologist (Carole Franck), the film retraces her life from the age of eight. As a girl (played by Cyrille Mairesse), Odette loves to dance and draw, and she trusts the adults around her, including Gilbert Miguié (Deladonchamps), a friend of her parents who proposes that they "play tickles". The family friend begins to sexually abuse her, a tragedy that upends her life and is made worse by a toxic home environment shaped by her mother Mado (Viard), with whom communication proves impossible; Cornillac plays her father, Fabrice. As an adult, Odette throws herself body and soul into her career as a dancer and into the whirl of life, with her best friend Manu (Gringe), her partner Lenny (Montel) and her dance teacher Madame Malec (Ascaride), as she tries to confront her past and reckon with the anger it left behind.

The film premiered in the Un Certain Regard section of the 2018 Cannes Film Festival on 14 May and was released in France on 14 November 2018, distributed by Orange Studio and UGC. At the Deauville American Film Festival Bescond and Métayer received the d'Ornano-Valenti Prize, and the film also won the best film prize in the Voilà! section of the Hamburg Film Festival. French critics were enthusiastic: Le Point and La Croix both called it a punch in the gut, the latter praising how it reconstructs the meanders of its director's recovery with virtuosity, while Télérama described it as a lively tale of resilience and joie de vivre and a tour de force. It received five nominations at the 2019 César Awards, winning Best Adaptation and Best Supporting Actress for Viard.

Holly and Richard drive out to his imposing country house so that she can meet, for the first time, the children of his previous marriage: the teenagers Lucia (Gotobed) and Ralph (Rolfe) and their younger sister Anna (Chapman). Anna, wide-eyed and winning, plays the gracious hostess, while the two older children barely acknowledge their father or their new stepmother. The atmosphere is uncomfortable from the start. Richard's estranged former wife, the children's mother, is nowhere to be found on the sprawling property; according to a text sent to Richard, she left the children alone on the assurance that the couple would soon arrive, an explanation that seems suspicious. At Richard's encouragement the children slaughter a goose before Holly's eyes, and at dinner even the youngest is allowed champagne. From the following day, oddity turns into menace: doors are locked, the children engage in strange rituals such as burying a doll deep in the woods, and they seem to share a frightening secret to which only they hold the key. Richard, who first presents himself as a loving father and husband, gradually reveals a more brutish side, and the story evolves into a portrait of family trauma, with Holly as the anxious outsider whose disbelief turns to terror.

Kara Gentry (McCormick) and Jessie Wilkins (Sharbino) are strangers from very different worlds who meet by chance on a flight from Vermont to Stillwater, Oklahoma. They discover that they are in the same situation: each is travelling to spend Christmas with family members she has never known. Kara, who comes from wealth, longs to be normal, while Jessie, who comes from more modest circumstances, wants a home, so the girls decide to swap identities. Kara is picked up by Jessie's grandmother Judy (Long), a goofy, hippie-like woman, and is nervous to discover that they are also collecting Jessie's father Jim (Rooney), who fortunately has never seen his daughter, allowing the charade to continue as she settles in with the Wilkins family. Jessie, meanwhile, finds herself in a mansion with the affluent Gentrys, where Kara's snobbish, materialistic grandmother Elsa (Derek) tries to mould her into a copy of herself, entering her in a beauty pageant she once won, while Elsa's husband Bob (Rich) grows tired of his wife's controlling ways. What began as a lark becomes complicated as each girl grows close to the family she is deceiving, and the two struggle to find a way to tell the truth. Matters come to a head when Kara's father Jeff (Kane) and his fiancée arrive to surprise her, only to see her at the pageant being announced as Jessie, and the revelations that follow help two broken families begin to mend.

Reviews were mild. The Movie Buff's Matt DeCristo found it predictable, with a straight-to-video feel, clumsy exposition and a contrived ending, but charming, crediting the two leads' sense of fun and the effective performances of Long and Derek. Scared Stiff Reviews rated it 6.5 out of 10, calling it a decent film that follows the Christmas formula with a be-grateful-for-what-you-have message, and Common Sense Media noted its themes of being true to oneself and the importance of family.

Years after humanity's war with the alien alliance known as the Covenant, a fragile peace holds. Locke and his Office of Naval Intelligence team are sent to the colony world of Sedra to track a possible Covenant infiltration. Following an alien smuggler, they confront a Sangheili zealot who detonates a device in a crowded shopping center, releasing a mysterious element that attacks only human DNA and kills many people, including the daughter of Colonel Randall Aiken (Steven Waddington). Locke learns that the substance comes from Alpha Halo, a fragment of the ring world destroyed years earlier, now orbiting a star so closely that its surface becomes lethally hot by day,.

Locke and Aiken lead a joint team to the fragment to gather proof that the Covenant has broken the treaty and to destroy the source with a HAVOK nuclear warhead before sunrise. After they capture two smugglers, their dropship is brought down by swarms of Lekgolo worms drawn to active technology, and the survivors must cross the hostile terrain in darkness. As members are devoured one by one and the smugglers' two-seat ship becomes the only way off, the group fractures. Horrigan and Ramos mutiny and try to flee with a smuggler, and both are killed. Locke, Aiken and Private Talitha Macer reach the dropship and retrieve the bomb, which must be triggered by hand, and they draw lots to decide who stays behind. Aiken secretly rigs the draw, sacrifices himself to lure away the worms, and Locke and Macer escape as the fragment is destroyed at dawn.

Filmed in Iceland and Northern Ireland, Nightfall premiered weekly from 11 November to 10 December 2014 for owners of Halo: The Master Chief Collection on Xbox before a wider release in 2015. It won a Golden Reel Award for sound editing, though some critics called it cheap-looking and its soldiers interchangeable.

The featurette examines the production of the first season of the FX horror anthology series created by Ryan Murphy and Brad Falchuk, later subtitled Murder House, which aired from October to December 2011. That season follows the Harmon family, Vivien (Connie Britton), Ben (Dylan McDermott) and their teenage daughter Violet (Taissa Farmiga), who move from Boston to Los Angeles in an attempt to repair a marriage damaged by a miscarriage and infidelity. They settle in a restored mansion known to locals as the "Murder House", unaware that it is haunted by the ghosts of its former residents and their victims.

Combining behind-the-scenes footage with interviews, the documentary has co-creator and executive producer Falchuk explain the genesis of the project and how its many strange ideas came together into a dramatic horror series. The principal actors, among them Britton, McDermott, Farmiga, Jessica Lange, Evan Peters, Denis O'Hare and Alexandra Breckenridge, discuss the show and their characters, while members of the creative team, including producer Alexis Martin Woodall, set and costume designers, make-up artists and visual effects artists, describe how the distinctive look of the series was achieved. The film covers the show's inspirations, themes, characters, locations, sets, make-up and visual effects.

Reviewers of the Blu-ray gave the featurette a generally favourable mention. Steven Cohen of High-Def Digest described it as a fairly comprehensive look at the show's production and recommended that fans take a look, while noting that co-creator Ryan Murphy was conspicuously absent. Bloody Disgusting's review of the set likewise remarked that Murphy's absence stood out sharply, especially as the other participants spent part of their time on camera talking about him.

Structured as a chronological portrait, the film opens with Williams improvising a torrent of logical nonsense when asked on Inside the Actors Studio how his mind works. It traces his childhood as an only child, with step-brothers he scarcely knew, an outrageous mother and a cold father, his first taste of laughter when he impersonated a teacher in high school, and his time at Juilliard under John Houseman. It follows his explosive rise in the comedy clubs of late-1970s Los Angeles and his instant stardom on Mork & Mindy, alongside the drug, alcohol and sexual excesses that followed and the death of John Belushi, which frightened him into sobriety. It covers the failure of Popeye, the end of his first marriage to Valerie Velardi and his relationship with Marsha Garces, and revisits highlights such as an improvised speech he gave at the 2003 Critics' Choice Awards. The final part touches on his heart attack, his Parkinson's disease diagnosis and his final years, though without fully explaining his death. Interviewees include Billy Crystal, Whoopi Goldberg, David Letterman, Steve Martin, Pam Dawber, Eric Idle, Elayne Boosler, Bobcat Goldthwait, Lewis Black, Velardi and his son Zak Williams.

Brian (Smyth) is a very intelligent nine-year-old who has grown up in a non-Christian home. While writing a school paper about the Pilgrims, he learns about their faith, and after a supernatural encounter with God he sets out on a quest to find out more about what Christians believe. He meets heavy opposition from the world around him, above all from his father Simon (Lindquist), an atheist television newscaster. His father even forbids him to read the Bible, but Brian persists in seeking God and finds allies in the pastor of a local church (Brimley) and a wounded U.S. Marine (London) who has lost a leg. Brian's pure and innocent faith leads him to pray for the veteran and to send a woman home to pray for her blind baby, and the manifestations of God's power that follow quickly become breaking news. When a reporter tries to make a mockery of the boy's faith, Brian's family faces severe tests and trials. The story takes a darker turn when the mob becomes involved: a contract is put out on Brian's life, a little girl is shot in his place and healed through prayer, and Brian is kidnapped by a man who wants him to pray for his own son, before being returned. These events lead to what the film presents as one of the greatest miracles of all, especially for Brian's own family.

Summer '03 is a 2018 American coming-of-age comedy-drama written and directed by Becca Gleason in her feature debut. Joey King stars as sixteen-year-old Jamie Winkle, with Jack Kilmer as Luke, Andrea Savage as her mother Shira, Paul Scheer as her father Ned, June Squibb as her grandmother Dotty, and Erin Darke, Kelly Lamor Wilson, Stephen Ruffin and Logan Medina in supporting roles. The cinematography is by Ben Hardwicke, the editing by Josie Azzam and the music by Nathan Matthew David.

In the summer of 2003, Jamie's family is thrown into turmoil when her manipulative, anti-Semitic grandmother Dotty, on her deathbed, summons each relative in turn and hands out insults, outrageous advice and long-buried secrets before dying contentedly. The revelations set off a chain of chaos. Jamie's father learns that he never knew his biological father and abandons the family to track him down, returning days later with an ailing German man who insults Jamie's Jewish mother. Jamie's younger cousin Dylan (Medina), told by Dotty to seek out a gay conversion camp, steals his parents' car and nearly gets himself killed. Dotty's most pointed instruction to Jamie concerns sex, a subject her more experienced friend Emily (Wilson) is happy to explain. Searching for meaning during a summer of bad choices, Jamie neglects her devoted friend March (Ruffin), who is in love with her, and begins a secret fling with Luke, a seminary student eager to sample worldly pleasures before his ordination who says he chose the priesthood for its job security. Grounded by her clueless parents and torn between guilt and desire, Jamie finally confronts the family's hypocrisy in a frank monologue at Dotty's funeral, pointing out that her grandmother disliked her mother simply for being Jewish.

Dawn of a New Era covers the making of the original film and the direction the filmmakers first intended to take before realising that computer-generated imagery was the way to go, along with recollections of working with Stan Winston's effects team, surviving a real hurricane during the shoot and working with Spielberg. Making Prehistory looks more closely at the filming, particularly the animatronic Tyrannosaurus and Velociraptors, the origins of the dinosaur sounds and the animatics, while The Next Step in Evolution discusses the computer-generated images and digital composites created by Industrial Light & Magic, the sound effects and the score, and Spielberg's input while he was in the middle of filming Schindler's List. Finding the Lost World explains that a sequel was always at the back of Spielberg's mind, and that once novelist Michael Crichton had published a follow-up novel the filmmakers chose its much darker direction. Something Survived focuses on the sequel's technical side, including its ending, which was essentially written into the story on a whim. The Third Adventure has cast and crew reminiscing about working with Johnston, shooting on location and on soundstages, the practical effects and the choice of the Spinosaurus as the new villain.

High-Def Digest's M. Enois Duarte considered the series exhaustive, singling out the effects segment as a great watch for fans and the final installment as really interesting, especially for admirers of the third film.

Two drunken fishermen, Moss (Michael Prichard) and Stanley (Shepherd Stevenson), set out to catch a mermaid and succeed in hauling one (Alexandra Bokova) from the Pacific in their net. As she struggles to escape, one of them hacks off her tail with an axe and throws her human half into the fish hold. The scene is observed from a nearby yacht by the psychiatrist Dr. Beyer (Burt Culver), who swims aboard and kills the fishermen. Her seemingly helpful rescuer is in fact a demented doctor who sees her as the world's most valuable prize, and he locks her away in the Beyer Psychiatric Hospital, his institution for disturbed young women, where she recovers as a new pair of human legs grow. As "the new girl" she is mocked by some patients and pitied by others, and nobody believes she is a mermaid. Never speaking a word, she communicates through expression and sign language, and she befriends the Ghost (Meggan Kaiser), the spirit of a girl murdered by Beyer, whom one other patient can also see. Knowing that being away from the water will eventually kill her, the mermaid must rely on her survival instincts as Beyer's true nature becomes clear and the girls rally around her in a fight for their lives.

Reviews were mixed. Stuart D. Monroe of Horror DNA was enthusiastic, describing the film as a fantasy-horror fairy tale with a message of female empowerment, equal parts fantasy and arthouse, and calling Bokova's wordless performance hypnotic. Moria, by contrast, felt the premise had great potential but found Grellman's direction confusing, criticising the cramped house used for the asylum scenes, murky side plots and the psychiatrist's poorly motivated actions.

In the near future, ten convicts on death row are chosen to take part in the Jurassic Games, a televised virtual reality competition broadcast to a huge international audience. Plugged into a simulated world of deserts and jungles, the contestants must survive attacks by digital dinosaurs as well as each other. Only one of them can emerge as the winner and earn freedom; the catch is that anyone who dies inside the game dies in the real world as well. Tucker insists that he is an innocent man and is determined to survive so he can return to his children, who watch him on television as he fights for his life. His fellow contestants include Joy, a teenage psychopath, and a cartel boss, and their backstories are filled in as the competition goes on. Presiding over the spectacle is the flamboyant Host, who wears a sharp suit and a black dinosaur helmet, while the ruthless Savannah runs the show behind the scenes. The film repeatedly cuts away to viewers laughing at the carnage, and its story includes twists involving the characters' motives.

The film was released on DVD in the United States and United Kingdom in May 2018. Critics treated it as a mockbuster drawing on Jurassic Park, The Hunger Games, Death Race, The Matrix and Battle Royale. Luiz H. C. of Bloody Disgusting called it shallow but a legitimately entertaining ride, finding its self-aware satire of reality television better than expected and some of its dinosaur sequences surprisingly impressive, though the characters were one-dimensional; he singled out Hampton as a solid lead and Merriman as the most entertaining character. Zoe Crombie of Film Inquiry also praised Merriman's scene-stealing performance and Burgess's over-the-top turn, but criticized the weightless computer-generated creatures, uncreative cinematography, contradictory satire of violent media and reliance on racial stereotypes, concluding that it was less than the sum of its borrowed parts.

Anders Baasmo Christiansen returns as Roy Gundersen, a man who loves racing American cars, legally or otherwise. He is on his way to Møre og Romsdal to marry his longtime girlfriend Sylvia (Kathrine Thorborg Johansen, replacing the actress from the earlier films) at the top of the Trollstigen mountain road, but a series of problems arises before the wedding can take place. On the eve of the ceremony, as friends and family celebrate among gleaming muscle cars, Sylvia's old friend Robin (Alexandra Maria Lara) turns up in a red Porsche, and a drunken Roy kisses her. At the wedding the next day Robin exposes his lapse, drives off with Sylvia and the couple's baby, and challenges Roy to race her for his bride at the famous Nürburgring circuit in Germany, one of the longest and most demanding tracks in the world. Roy sets out through Sweden and Denmark to Germany with his regular helpers, his daughter Nina (Ida Husøy), Doffen (Sven Nordin), Nybakken (Otto Jespersen) and TT (Trond Halbo). Along the way two of them travel in a restored vintage hearse and accidentally pick up a corpse, the gang runs into two other men named Roy, which causes a string of mix-ups, and they clash with Lemmy Müller (Henning Baum), a German hot-rodder with a striking resemblance to Motörhead's Lemmy Kilmister. Henrik Mestad, Peter Kurth, Milan Peschel and Ruby O. Fee also appear.

At home it was voted one of three finalists for the audience award at the 2021 Amanda Awards, and a fourth film was later planned. International critics were harsh. Decider's John Serba called the race-for-the-bride premise a rickety jalopy, finding the chase sequences forgettable and marred by dated computer graphics and the jokes dead on arrival, while Jonathon Wilson of Ready Steady Cut dismissed it as absolute garbage, ridiculing its PlayStation 2-era effects and gags that never work.

The film traces Houston's life from her childhood in Newark, New Jersey, where she was nicknamed Nippy, grew up surrounded by music and learned to sing in church under her demanding mother, a professional singer. It follows her early work as a model and backing vocalist, her signing with Clive Davis's Arista Records and her record-breaking debut album, as well as her close bond with her friend Robyn Crawford, the rumours this provoked and the family's control of her business, led by her father John. It examines the criticism that her pop music was not black enough, her marriage to Bobby Brown, the birth of her daughter Bobbi Kristina, her celebrated Super Bowl national anthem, the global success of The Bodyguard and her 1994 concerts in post-apartheid South Africa. Darker chapters follow: drug use that began in her teens with her brother Michael, a lawsuit from her own father, failing health and voice, repeated stays in rehab and her death in 2012. Most strikingly, the film reports that Houston and her brother Gary were sexually abused as children by a relative, and that Whitney named Dee Dee Warwick as her abuser.

French, a British martial artist living in Los Angeles, is struggling to pay the bills on his dojo. Financially desperate, he turns to an underworld connection, Mad Alex, a student at the dojo who works for Tommy's debt collection operation. Tommy takes French on and pairs him with Sue, a hard-drinking, washed-up enforcer who has been doing low-level collections for decades. The story unfolds over a single weekend.

On their first day, the two set out together in a Cadillac, visiting debtors and developing a system for their shakedowns, including a scale for judging how likely each visit is to turn violent. Sue keeps up a steady stream of verbal abuse as he takes the newcomer under his wing, but gradually reveals a damaged soul beneath his drunken exterior, while French's fighting skills are tested in a series of escalating brawls. As the weekend goes on, the stakes rise when Tommy sends them on a job for the notorious Barbosa. Their final assignment leads them to a barkeeper with a secret, forcing French to choose between finishing the job and doing the right thing, and events escalate toward a gritty, emotional and risky climax that changes the fates of both men.

In Yonebayashi's 18-minute fantasy adventure "Kanini & Kanino", two tiny freshwater crab siblings live with their father, Toto, in a stream while their mother, Kaka, is away giving birth. When their father suddenly disappears, leaving them alone, Kanini and Kanino set out on a perilous journey to find him. The characters speak only an invented language, and the music is by Takatsugu Muramatsu, the director's collaborator on When Marnie Was There and Mary and the Witch's Flower.

Momose's 16-minute drama "Life Ain't Gonna Lose", scored by Masanori Shimada in his first film work, follows Shun Yashima, a young boy born with a life-threatening allergy to eggs. His family's daily life revolves around protecting him: he must eat special meals at school, his classmates must take care not to spread egg-tainted saliva, and even a school trip requires careful planning, while his mother tries to keep up her career as a dance teacher. One day, while his parents are away, Shun accidentally eats something containing egg.

Yamashita's 13-minute action short "Invisible", with music by Yasutaka Nakata, follows a man who is literally overlooked by everyone around him. Ignored throughout his day, he begins to lose his physical hold on the world, until an unexpected encounter with a stranger, a blind old man, gives him a sudden chance to become a hero.

The anthology was originally planned with a fourth segment by Ghibli director Isao Takahata, but it was reduced to three after his death in April 2018. Its ending theme, "Chiisana Eiyū", is sung by Kaela Kimura. The film was released in Japan on 24 August 2018 and in North America by GKIDS on 10 January 2019, with an English cast including Maggie Q and Liam O'Brien, and it later streamed worldwide on Netflix.

Skyler is a talented but untrained street dancer who has long lived in the shadow of her formally trained sister Tosha, whom the family regards as the real dancer. Her hardworking mother dismisses her passion and pushes her to enroll in medical assistant school instead. When Skyler learns of a dance competition whose winner will receive a full college scholarship, she decides to chase her dream regardless of her family's doubts. She tries out for the same crew as her sister, one of the city's two leading hip-hop teams, the Pulsars, run by the demanding Jada, where she is a long shot surrounded by established performers, including a rival determined to sabotage anyone in her path. Because each team may send only one member to compete for the scholarship, Skyler practices relentlessly in the underground dance scene. There she meets Tyrell, Jada's estranged son and a gifted dancer, and his encouragement helps her push her style to another level and overcome her persistent self-doubt, while her mother eventually comes to recognize what she had underestimated in her daughter.

The film was released on DVD and digital platforms in the United States on 3 April 2018. Elvin Ross composed the music, and the film is rated PG-13 for suggestive content and some language. Reviews were mixed: critics generally praised the energetic choreography and Taylor's presence while faulting the predictable story and uneven acting. Common Sense Media's Renee Longstreet noted that the dancing stays at the center of the film, calling that both its strength and its weakness, and observed that the franchise's enthusiastic fan base seems undeterred by thin plots.

On New Year's Eve, a group of five friends, three young men and two women, decide to celebrate at the top of a mountain for an unforgettable experience, and make their way to an old funicular. Things go wrong from the start: Katya's boyfriend Kirill suddenly refuses to board the cable car, while she refuses to get off, so the rest of the group rides up with her. The car stops unexpectedly, then starts moving again when the power returns, so when it halts a second time nobody thinks much of it and they begin celebrating the New Year right there. By the morning of 1 January, however, the car still has not moved, and they realize they are stuck high above an abyss with no way to call for help. At first they expect rescue to come, and they light a fire with whatever rubbish they can find to keep warm, but it soon dies out along with their hope. Cold, height and the fear of a slow death bring out their basest survival instincts. An attempt to climb down the cable ends when one of them falls into a crevice hidden beneath the snow, and as the remaining friends lose hope, a struggle for survival breaks out inside the car, revealing who they really are.

Inspired by real events of the early eighteenth century, the story follows Ivan Demarin (Ilya Malanin), a young officer of Peter the Great's new guards, who on the Tsar's orders travels to Tobolsk, the frontier capital of the Siberian province deep in the forest. There he falls in love for the first time with Masha Remezova (Yuliya Makarova), the daughter of the renowned Siberian chronicler, cartographer and architect Semyon Remezov (Dmitri Nazarov). Ivan and his regiment become caught up in a conspiracy of local princes hunting for gold, and the young lovers take part in Colonel Ivan Bukhholts's expedition of 1714 to 1716 in search of the trading town of Yarkand in Kashgaria and the gold fields beyond. On the edge of the Kazakh steppes the expedition founds the Yamyshev fortress, where the army winters, only for it to be besieged by hordes of Dzungars from Central Asia with no one to call for help. Dmitriy Dyuzhev plays Peter the Great and Ekaterina Guseva the future Empress Catherine I, while Andrey Burkovskiy and Agata Mutsenietse appear as Swedish and German prisoners of war, with Evgeniy Dyatlov as the Siberian governor Prince Matvei Gagarin.

Years have passed since the magic mirror portal shattered, scattering shards across the world. Each fragment is a gateway to a different fairy-tale realm with its own timelines, part of a vast multiverse, and an organization called Looking Glass has been formed to combat threats from those kingdoms. Alice, whose sanity is kept in check by medicine prepared by the Hatter, guards the shards, while the fairy-tale princesses and Red Riding Hood, an archer combining the look of the storybook heroine with the skills of Robin Hood, work to collect them so that they can rebuild the portal and return home.

Prince Charming, who survived Rumpelstiltskin's attempt on his life, is on the run from Magda, the power-hungry ruler of Atlantis, and washes up near a large city. Magda follows and unleashes her soldiers from the sea, hoping to force him to marry her, because whoever weds the prince and wears his ring will gain infinite power and rule the world. To fight back, Alice has the Hatter thaw Snow White from a block of ice, and the heroines, reunited after a brawl with Magda's followers in a warehouse, are astonished to find her alive. Rumpelstiltskin, meanwhile, manipulates Magda into an alliance in exchange for control of Atlantis. When the heroines find the prince, Snow White shields his escape with a wall of ice, but Rumpelstiltskin overpowers him and takes his appearance. Magda then uses her magic to cast the princesses into separate dimensions that warp space and time; once they find each other again, they set out for the realm beyond the mirror to stop Magda's wedding to the prince.

Shot in downtown Los Angeles, the film was released direct to DVD in the United States on 1 May 2018. Critics were unkind, with the German magazine Cinema calling it even sillier than its predecessor.

Marriage counsellor William (Auret) and his wife Suzanne have set up a kind of adventure camp for couples on Corazon Island, a small Pacific island, combining physical challenges with relationship counselling to help heal dysfunctional marriages. As William puts the latest group through the course, Suzanne announces that she wants a divorce, leaving him to carry on with the remaining couples. Nearby lies a former shark research station, a floating laboratory just offshore where classified government experiments have been carried out. The group soon comes under attack from the result: a six-headed shark that kills one couple after another. Trapped on the island with minimal weapons, the survivors try to fight back, but they discover that the creature has enormous strength and an almost unstoppable ability to regenerate its heads when they are cut off, and that it can even move onto land by walking on its heads, so that no one is safe in the water or on the beach. In the end only William and Mary (Thandi Sebe) remain, and they finally defeat the shark by blowing it up with gas cylinders.

Moria's reviewer found that the series never reaches the tongue-in-cheek heights of the Sharknado films and that its only gimmick is adding heads, though Atkins does a serviceable job and the scene of the shark walking up the beach provides a moment of delirious silliness; the review faulted the effects as ranging from semi-competent to slipshod, the cheap-looking laboratory and several weak performances, including Auret's in the lead. In December 2019 the German channel Tele 5 screened the film in its series The Worst Movies of All Time.

A few hundred miles west of Hawaii, a Russian submarine is secretly tapping an American communications cable when the noise of its drilling awakens a gigantic prehistoric shark, which tears the vessel apart. Ivanov escapes into the bow with three crew members, abandoning the others. The US Navy destroyer Shaw finds the wreck, and Lynch dives in the submersible she designed, rescuing the Russians, who claim to be whale researchers, before the shark swallows the submersible whole. Admiral King wants to cut the crew loose to protect the ship, but Streeper insists on a rescue, and the loyal crew locks the admiral in his cabin. Cheng rigs an anchor with high-voltage current as bait; when the shark opens its mouth, the submersible escapes, and the jolt appears to stop the creature, though one sailor dies in the electrified water.

Under questioning, Popov admits the Russians were on an intelligence mission. Ivanov breaks free, arms a comrade and kills the tactical adviser Jameson, while the shark resurfaces and devours a yacht. Cheng turns the submersible into a bomb, but Ivanov forces her to throw the detonator overboard, and the backup remote she builds only works at close range. Streeper orders the crew into the lifeboats and prepares to go down with his ship, and Lynch swims back to help him. King, freed from his cabin, kills Ivanov in a shootout but is mortally wounded, and when the shark crashes through the hull, he detonates the explosives, destroying the beast and the destroyer as the survivors salute him.

The exterior shipboard scenes were filmed aboard the SS Lane Victory, a World War II vessel now serving as a museum ship in San Pedro, California. A sequel, Megalodon Rising, followed in 2021.

Walter Cooke (Jacobus) is a blind man living in a modern American city, an apple pie enthusiast with a knack for sensing danger. Underestimated and brushed aside by a local gang while shopping at his neighbourhood grocery, he comes to the aid of its owner Gordon (Yuan), his friend, who is deep in debt to the gangsters. Surprising both Gordon and the thugs with his physical abilities, Walter sends them packing in an alley fight in which he puts his white cane to good use. This is where the original short ended and where The Game picks up. Following the gangsters back to their boss, Sal (Bucaro), Walter and Gordon get further into trouble, and elements of Gordon's own past come to light in connection with the villains. The stakes rise, but Walter has an ace up his sleeve, and the confrontation eventually leads the pair to take on the toughs in their own warehouse, where Gordon must fight alongside Walter against an array of opponents armed with guns and blades. Walter himself remains something of an enigma, with hints of a deeper history left for possible future stories.

Reviewers from action-focused outlets welcomed it as a homage to the blind swordsman genre, especially Zatoichi and Blind Fury. Cinapse called it enjoyable, praising the basic character work that adds heart and comedy between the set pieces and Jacobus's physical and comedic talents, and recommended it to action devotees and fans of the sub-genre. Film Combat Syndicate praised its blend of slapstick and intense fight scenes and its warm portrayal of Walter and Gordon's friendship, while noting that the short format leaves Walter's background largely unexplored.

Ellie is a career-driven city planner who enjoys a busy urban life. Just weeks before Christmas, she is called home to help on her family's poinsettia farm because her father has hurt his back and cannot keep up during the busiest season of the year. The family business must deliver tens of thousands of plants for the town's annual Christmas parade, but on arrival Ellie discovers that the real problem is worse: the poinsettias are still green and have yet to turn red. Her parents admit that this is why they really needed her, since she has always had a special touch with the plants. Ellie initially clashes with Sean, a handsome botanist who now works on the farm, spends much of his time with her family and spills dirt on her cashmere coat when they first meet, and she blames him for the problem. As the two try new fertilizer, adjust the watering and argue over the thermostat, they grow closer. Complications come from Patty, Ellie's childhood rival and now a local lifestyle personality with her own show, who is dating Sean and offers to buy the farm. Ellie eventually realizes that the town's new development is to blame: the city lights at night are preventing the plants from changing color. The poinsettias turn red in time, but Ellie must still decide whether her future lies in the city or back home with her roots and the man she has fallen for.

The film premiered on Lifetime during the 2018 holiday season. Reviewers found it light and predictable but pleasant. Very Merry Movies called it an enjoyable, quick-paced film that was not too schmaltzy and that far exceeded its title, praising Lenz while regretting that the rivalry with Patty was shallow and that the story had too little Christmas in it, likening it to an HGTV episode crossed with a Hallmark movie. Patrick Serrano of Lifetime Uncorked gave it a rating of two Christmas trees, poking fun at its montages and formula.

At its core, the film is a poignant exploration of the human cost of conflict, shedding light on the experiences of ordinary men who were thrust into extraordinary circumstances. It highlights the camaraderie and bonds that formed among soldiers in the trenches, as well as the trauma and PTSD that many struggled with upon their return home.

The film also touches on themes of nostalgia, memory, and the passage of time, as the veterans' recollections serve as a window into a bygone era. The archival footage, which has been meticulously restored and presented in a cinematic format, adds to the sense of immediacy and intimacy, drawing the viewer into the world of the soldiers.

Ultimately, They Shall Not Grow Old is a powerful tribute to the men who served during World War I, and a reminder of the enduring impact that their experiences have had on our collective understanding of war and its effects on individuals.

The short fills in an event that happens off-screen during Incredibles 2. In the feature, Edna volunteers to babysit Jack-Jack after learning that the infant has developed a wide range of superpowers, and returns him to his family with a suit designed to accommodate them. Auntie Edna reveals what happened that night at her mansion. Bob drops Jack-Jack off, and in her workshop Edna lets the baby loose so she can observe his many abilities, which include teleportation, shrinking, anti-gravity and multiplying into several copies, as well as his "demon baby" form; the short also accounts for elements set up in the film, such as the Mozart music and the cookies. In a lab sequence, the roles are reversed: Jack-Jack takes charge while Edna watches from inside an observation chamber, first fascinated even as her lab is wrecked, then bored and restless, until she simply waits for things to calm down. Once the baby is worn out, she sets about designing the seemingly impossible: a super suit that can harness all of his powers.

Mathot said he wanted to push the always-in-control Edna out of her comfort zone without losing the essence of a character very close to Bird, using time cuts and classical music for the lab sequence; Bird encouraged him to add more powers and quicken the timing. The film was completed in about four and a half months by a crew of roughly 40 artists. Following the precedent of Jack-Jack Attack, the short included on the home video release of The Incredibles, it was released with Incredibles 2 on digital platforms on 23 October 2018 and on Blu-ray and DVD on 6 November 2018. Reviewers welcomed it as a fun bonus for fans, praising its colorful animation, Jack-Jack's imaginative powers and the rare sight of Edna losing her composure, and enjoying the glimpse into her mansion and workspace.

Elizabeth Bennett (Lowndes), a New York event planner, is invited by her college friend George (Gleason), now the young mayor of the small Connecticut town of Lambton, to organise its Christmas festival. George secretly hopes to rekindle a romance, as his assistant Jane (McCormick) can plainly tell. On arriving, Elizabeth clashes with Travis (Estus), an assistant who cuts the coffee line for his boss, and then scolds the man waiting in the car, the high-profile billionaire William Darcy (Rady). When a water main break sends the town gazebo into a sinkhole, Elizabeth proposes holding the festival at Pemberley Manor, the picturesque estate she drove past on her way into town, only to discover that it belongs to Darcy, who lacks holiday spirit and is in the process of selling it to developers who plan to replace it with condos. After she persuades the buyers to back the idea, Darcy agrees to help on condition that his name is kept out of the publicity and funds the decorations. Elizabeth brings Christmas into the long-empty house, and a montage of tree trimming, cookie decorating and a sleigh ride reveals that Darcy, who lost his parents, once loved the season. When the festival soloist falls ill, Elizabeth steps in to sing "O Holy Night", and the unlikely pair begin to fall for each other, while new complications arise from a rival suitor in George and someone trying to take over the festival planning.

Reviews were generally warm. Paul Carlson of Escape Into Film gave it four out of five, praising Lowndes and Rady's chemistry and the way the film plays with two iconic literary characters without forcing in the plot of the novel. 18 Cinema Lane scored it 8.2 out of 10, appreciating that both of Elizabeth's suitors are good people, while finding little resemblance to Pride and Prejudice. Very Merry Movies thought the love story felt flat and the Austen connection confusing, though it enjoyed the side romance between Jane and Travis.

Katie, who once came close to competing at the Olympics, now manages a touring Christmas ice show starring her friend Jessica, and the two hope that the earnings from the tour will let them buy an ice rink back home in New Jersey. Their final stop is San Senova, whose king, Alexander, is struggling to live up to the legacy of his late father, who founded the kingdom's beloved holiday traditions, and has been nicknamed a Grinch after the press criticized his lack of Christmas spirit. Katie literally bumps into him at the Christmas market without realizing who he is. After the show, Princess Christina, a talented but insecure young skater, asks the two women for lessons and persuades her father to let her stage a Christmas skating pageant at the palace rink. Alexander hires Katie and Jessica for a large fee that would fund their dream, and invites them to stay at the palace. As Katie prepares the pageant, encourages Christina and helps the king rediscover the joy of the season, from decorating a tree to making handmade gifts for his staff and baking cookies for the royal Christmas tea, she and Alexander fall in love, while Jessica and Nicholas begin their own romance. But the tradition-loving people of San Senova may not accept a foreigner as their queen, and when Jessica is injured and their rink deal is threatened, Katie must choose between her plans and the family she has come to love.

The fictional kingdom was created in Romania. Filming took place in October 2018 with Castel Film Studios in Bucharest, at locations including Snagov Palace on Lake Snagov, while the town of San Senova was built on a studio lot. Reviews were mixed. The Avocado's recap found the leading couple bland and Cooper's king monotone, preferring the secondary romance and pitying the moping princess, while other viewers enjoyed the warm chemistry between the leads and the Romanian palace scenery.

As Holly and Nick's paths cross, they embark on a journey of self-discovery and healing, learning to let go of their past heartaches and rediscover the magic of Christmas. Through their blossoming romance, the film highlights the importance of human connection, forgiveness, and the redemptive power of love.

The movie also touches on themes of grief, loss, and the challenges of single parenthood, showcasing Nick's unwavering dedication to his daughter and his own journey towards healing and finding happiness again. As Holly and Nick navigate their feelings for each other, they must confront their own emotional baggage and learn to trust themselves and others.

Ultimately, Christmas Wonderland is a feel-good film that celebrates the joy, hope, and renewal of the holiday season, reminding viewers that it's never too late to rediscover the magic of love and Christmas.

Steven (Bennett) is an all-business architect who is about to make partner at his firm if he can win over a major new client, and who even questions a colleague's festive tie. He has a painful meet-cute in his office lobby with Gretchen (PenaVega), a stager for a catalogue company who dreams of turning her hobby of holiday decorating into a business of her own, and who has covered the lobby in garlands and fake snow. When Steven learns that emergency construction work on his sister's house means his whole family will spend Christmas at his place, he panics: he does not even own a string of lights, and they are expecting a perfectly decorated home. He hires Gretchen to transform his bare house, and when the family arrives and is delighted, he persuades her to stay on as his family's Christmas activity coordinator, dangling the chance to become the official decorator for his company's properties. While Steven retreats into his work, Gretchen leads the family through picking out a tree, decorating, making mulled cider at her aunt's inn, personalised stockings and cookie decorating. Her expert Christmas spirit brings the family together; she mediates a squabble between Steven, his sister and her husband and his parents, and counsels his niece, who wants to be a singer rather than a doctor as her father expects. Gradually Steven is drawn back into family life, and he and Gretchen, both single and with her parents no longer living, grow closer. Meanwhile a demanding client rejects Steven's designs, and when a great opportunity presents itself to Gretchen, the two must decide what is really important in life.

Reviewers found it light, feel-good holiday fare. Fits of Fury thought the premise of hiring a "Christmas ambassador" bizarre, but singled out PenaVega for the film's best and funniest moments and her character's gumption, and credited the easy chemistry between the leads as a large reason the film works. The Avocado's tongue-in-cheek recap poked fun at the décor, the fake Christmas tree and the clichéd plot.

Clara is the manager of the restaurant at the Thunder Mountain Ski Resort, a job she took after her attempt at running her own restaurant in Chicago failed. This Christmas the resort is abuzz because her boss, Mr. Peters, has hired Shane, a celebrity chef who won the reality cooking competition Can You Stand the Heat?, as the new head chef. Clara is not especially excited at first and is focused on getting resettled, but with the encouragement of her pushy best friend Bonnie she and the soft-spoken Shane quickly connect over their shared passion for cooking. Both, however, are keeping secrets. Shane has his own mysterious reason for taking the job, linked to a photograph he keeps and to the place where his parents once spent a happy Christmas.
