Clara still dreams of having her own kitchen, and Mr. Peters asks her to persuade Frank and Jackie Haven, the couple who run the nearby Mountain View Inn and treat her like the daughter they never had, to sell their property to him. When Clara, Bonnie and Clive break in to find the real plans for the inn, she discovers that her boss may not be as kindly as she believed, and her ambitions and Shane's revelation threaten their new romance.

The film was poorly received by reviewers of holiday movies. Jeffrey Lyles called it perhaps the laziest Christmas film of the year, faulting a generic script, weak chemistry between the leads, obvious green-screen work, slow pacing and the stunt casting of Fox, although he noted the director's attention to beautifully shot food. Very Merry Movies found it dull, with a central conflict that emerges far too late and almost nothing about Christmas, while acknowledging the appeal of Bonnie as a sidekick and the real snowy location. Dynamite Review likewise judged it bad, citing the leads' lack of chemistry.

Determined to become the "First Mayor on the Moon", Mayor Humdinger prepares a rocket launch on Adventure Beach with Harold's help, but the boy accidentally fires the rocket without his uncle. It misses the moon, strikes a passing meteor and sends it hurtling towards Adventure Bay. Alerted by Everest and Jake, Ryder and the pups clear the town before the meteor crashes harmlessly into the sand, and Chase, whom Ryder has put in charge of a team, doubts his own leadership. The meteor's golden energy soon gives the pups superpowers, from Chase's super speed and Rubble's super strength to Marshall's mighty heat and Everest's freezing sneeze, and Mayor Goodway puts the rock on display at City Hall. Harold, who has also gained powers that let him build gadgets, joins his uncle in a plan to steal the meteor and take over the city. After a first attempt is foiled, Ryder trusts Chase to lead the newly named Mighty Pups, but Harold uses a tractor beam to lift the meteor, carries it to the Lookout, traps Ryder inside and sends the tower soaring into the sky, then attacks in a giant robot. Under Chase's command the pups free one another, retrieve the meteor from the robot's backpack and, when the Lookout plunges back to Earth, use whirlwinds and a sand tornado to cushion its fall, saving Ryder. Their powers fade as the meteor loses its glow, and the rock is stored beneath the Lookout.

The Mighty Pups concept returned in later specials of the series, such as Mighty Pups, Super Paws and Mighty Pups, Charged Up.

Amelia is a career-focused Chicago app developer with little holiday spirit, who usually escapes the season with a solo trip to Turks and Caicos. When investors reject her new app, Christmas Assist, which automates gift-buying and card-sending, on the grounds that it lacks the true spirit of Christmas, and her boyfriend Brad breaks up with her because she will not spend the holidays with his family, she sees her childhood photo with Uncle Harry on an invitation to the Fly By Santa anniversary in her hometown, Christmas Creek. Harry, a pilot who runs the family inn, flies over the town dressed as Santa every Christmas Eve to deliver toys to children in remote communities, and Amelia was once his co-pilot, until a quarrel between Harry and her father over the family business split the family and led her parents to move away. Back in town without telling her parents, Amelia reunites with her childhood best friend Mike, now in search and rescue and Harry's new co-pilot, and with his young niece Scout. As she and Mike grow close through tree hunting, stargazing, gingerbread and snowball fights, Harry tentatively rekindles his romance with his ex-girlfriend Pamela. When Amelia's parents arrive, a tense family dinner reopens the feud, but her heartfelt appeal about family helps the brothers reconcile, inspires her to rethink her app around charity, and leads her and Mike to confess their love before the Christmas Eve flight.

Reviewers found it pleasant but conventional. Fits of Fury praised Anderson's expressive, gentle performance and Weber's portrayal of Harry's shame and regret, and found the Harry and Pamela storyline more satisfying than the central romance, but judged the decades-long family feud underdeveloped and its climax quickly dissipated, calling the film perfectly fine yet very forgettable. Lifetime Uncorked rated it three Christmas trees.

The story follows Ikeda, a young and skilled engineer who is part of an elite group known as the "Iron Fortress" unit. The Iron Fortress is a mobile fortress designed to fight against the Kabaneri, and Ikeda's team is tasked with defending the city from these monstrous creatures.

As the movie begins, we see Ikeda and his team preparing for battle against the Kabaneri. They are equipped with advanced steam-powered machinery and a variety of deadly weapons. The team is led by Captain Sasaki, who has a personal vendetta against the Kabaneri.

The battle against the Kabaneri is intense and brutal, with both sides suffering heavy losses. Ikeda's team fights valiantly, but they soon realize that their enemy is not just mindless monsters - it's also a complex and terrifying foe that can adapt to their tactics.

As the battle rages on, we see flashbacks of Ikeda's past, including his relationship with his sister, who was killed by the Kabaneri. This personal connection makes Ikeda even more determined to defeat the enemy.

The movie takes a dramatic turn when Ikeda discovers that the Kabaneri are not just mindless creatures - they're also being controlled by a mysterious figure known as "The Puppeteer". The Puppeteer is revealed to be a powerful and ancient being who has been manipulating the Kabaneri for centuries, using them to further its own goals.

Ikeda's team launches a final assault on the Kabaneri stronghold, determined to defeat The Puppeteer and put an end to the war. The battle is intense and chaotic, with both sides suffering heavy losses. In the end, Ikeda faces off against The Puppeteer in a one-on-one duel.

The ending of the movie is bittersweet and emotionally charged. Ikeda emerges victorious, but not without great cost. He realizes that the war has changed him forever, and that he will never be able to go back to his old life. The movie ends with Ikeda standing alone, looking out at the ruins of the city, a symbol of the devastating consequences of war.

Overall, Kabaneri of the Iron Fortress: The Battle of Unato is a gripping and emotionally charged film that explores themes of war, sacrifice, and the human condition. With its stunning animation and intense action sequences, it's a must-see for fans of science fiction and fantasy.

The story begins with Wade Wilson, aka Deadpool (Ryan Reynolds), who has been rescued from his prison cell by Cable (Josh Brolin) and brought back to the present day. However, upon arrival, Wade discovers that he is now in a reality where he never died after being shot by the villainous Ajax (Ed Skrein). In this reality, Wade is still alive and has become a successful mercenary.

Cable informs Wade that he must travel with him to find his daughter, Nebula (Zazie Beetz), who was taken from him as a child. Along the way, they are joined by Domino (Zazie Beetz) and Russell Collins (Julian Dennison), a young mutant with the ability to heal.

As they embark on their journey, Wade and Cable's relationship is put to the test as they disagree on how to handle their mission. Meanwhile, Ajax returns, seeking revenge against Wade for foiling his plans in the previous film.

Throughout their adventure, the group faces various obstacles, including a run-in with the villainous Vanisher (Bill Skarsgård) and a confrontation with the sinister organization known as the "Vanisher's" henchmen. Along the way, Wade also begins to form a bond with Russell, who becomes like a surrogate son to him.

As they near their destination, Wade and Cable's differences come to a head, leading to a dramatic showdown between the two. In the end, Wade is able to reconcile with his past and find closure with his daughter, Nebula.

The film concludes with Wade reflecting on his journey and the lessons he has learned about family, friendship, and redemption. The movie ends on a hopeful note, with Wade looking forward to a brighter future for himself and those around him.

Overall, Once Upon a Deadpool is a heartwarming and action-packed adventure that explores themes of family, loyalty, and self-discovery. With its witty humor, engaging characters, and thrilling action sequences, the film is a must-see for fans of the X-Men franchise and comedy enthusiasts alike.

Flora was once the star attraction of the struggling circus run by Henry (Arquette), but because of arthritis the elephant can no longer perform her tricks. Henry and his 14-year-old daughter Dawn (Ortega) hope that an elephant preserve will take her in, but at the last minute it turns them down, demanding a large donation the circus cannot afford. With a heavy heart Henry decides to have Flora put down, and knowing it would break Dawn's heart, since Flora was trained by her late mother, he sends the girl to her aunt. Dawn discovers the plan, and the night before Flora is due to be euthanised she sneaks the elephant out of the circus and sets off on foot for the preserve. Between them and safety lie some two hundred kilometres of woods, a raging river and the mountains. They are pursued not only by Henry and Isabella (Varela), his new partner and the circus's star performer, but also by two elephant hunters, and a crook sends his protégé Sebastian (Martinez), a young pickpocket, after them. Sebastian, however, has his heart in the right place and helps Dawn and Flora on their journey. Flora finally reaches the preserve and is taken in, thanks to donations raised by Isabella, who documented the search on social media; there Flora meets her daughter. Sebastian joins the circus, where Dawn becomes a rising star.

"Down" is an episode of the American horror anthology web series Into the Dark, the fifth installment of its first season. Directed by Daniel Stamm from a script by Kent Kubena, it premiered on Hulu on February 1, 2019, and stars Natalie Martinez as Jennifer and Matt Lauria as Guy, with Arnie Pantoja, Diane Sellers and Christina Leone. Set over a Valentine's Day holiday weekend, it is a claustrophobic thriller about two strangers trapped in an elevator.

On the evening before Valentine's Day, Jennifer and Guy, who have both worked late in a high-rise office building, step into the same elevator on different floors. The car suddenly stops, apparently because of a storm, and with no phone signal they fear being stuck until Tuesday, since Monday is Presidents' Day. At first they get along well, sharing water, wine and chocolates and sketching each other. They agree to tell their raciest stories, and Jennifer records Guy on her phone as he invents one, until his mood darkens and he stops. They have sex, after which Guy says he could fall in love with her, but Jennifer tells him it was casual and that she still has feelings for an ex.

Stung, Guy confesses that he is not an accountant but one of the building's security guards, that he has been stalking her and that he stopped the elevator with his key. When Jennifer threatens him with prison, he halts it again; in the struggle the key breaks, truly trapping them. They climb through the ceiling, and Jennifer tries to escape up a ladder, but he chases her and both fall back into the car. Jennifer ties him up and, threatening him with a cigar cutter, records his confession: his name is John Deakins, a former white-collar worker whose "invented" story was real, except that his companion died when he crashed his car; after six months in jail he could not rebuild his career and staged the elevator incident to relive his old life. Early on Monday, a guard named Eddie tries to free them, but John, having freed himself and knocked Jennifer out, kills him with the elevator, murders Eddie's girlfriend, wipes the security files and drives off with Jennifer in his trunk. When he opens it, she attacks him, rams him into a dumpster with his car and sets it ablaze with a lit cigar, killing him.

The two-part Origins, set after the events of Halo 3, has the artificial intelligence Cortana recount the history of the universe to the Master Chief in cryogenic sleep, from the Forerunners' struggle against the Flood to humanity's war with the alien Covenant, while reflecting on whether war will ever end. The Duel, rendered with a filter that makes each frame resemble a watercolour painting, tells the tragic story of an Arbiter on the Elite home world who defies the Prophets. Homecoming centres on the final mission of a Spartan, Odd One Out follows the clumsy Spartan 1337, Prototype tells the story of an elite soldier called Ghost, The Babysitter depicts an infiltration mission by a squad of ODST troopers and a Spartan, and The Package follows five Spartans who must recover a "package" from a Covenant fleet.

In a dilapidated near-future city plagued by crime and corruption, Caddock is a fiercely ambitious and unscrupulous district attorney whose convicts are executed on the spot in the courtroom. After a bust, he takes possession of a chip containing technology belonging to The Night, a criminal gang led by Talen whose members are given cyborg enhancements. Caddock has just bought a new black luxury sedan, the Lazarus 1, and leaves the chip inside it after taking Daria, the object of his attentions, out to dinner. Members of The Night storm his office looking for the chip and throw him out of the window onto his own car. Rainer, a gruff cop who breaks the rules, investigates the killing. Soon afterwards the driverless car mysteriously comes to life, as if the dead man and his vehicle had become a single vengeful being, breaks out of impound and begins hunting down and killing the gang members responsible for the murder. Rainer, who has taken it on himself to protect Daria from the gang, joins forces with her to solve the mystery of the car, and in an homage to the original, Waits later refits the vehicle with the body of the 1977 car.

The film was poorly received. Kurt Dahlke of DVD Talk found Bowler and Munroe to have a fair amount of chemistry and praised one stunt sequence, but called the film daft, cliched and irritating, recommending it only as brain-dead entertainment if found cheaply. Moria gave it one star, criticizing Echternkamp for an action film in which the car does little but run people over, a sketchily developed future and contradictory explanations for the car, and named it the worst film of 2019.

Akane is a girl with no self-confidence. On the day before her birthday, her mother Midori sends her to collect her present from her aunt Chii, an outgoing antiques dealer whose boldness contrasts with Akane's timidity. At the shop they meet the mysterious alchemist Hippocrates and his tiny apprentice Pipo, who say they are on a mission to save their world. Through a passage from the basement they travel to Wonderland, a kingdom threatened by drought, where Akane is hailed as the Goddess of the Green Wind, the only one who can save it by helping the ailing crown prince of the rain kings perform the ceremony that renews the realm's water once every 600 years. A talisman that pulls her forward whenever she turns negative drags the reluctant Akane along. On the road the travellers clash with the menacing iron man Zan Gu and his sorcerer's apprentice, who are plotting to destroy the entrance to the great well, and Hippocrates is turned into a fly. In the capital, Akane learns that Zan Gu is in fact the prince himself, transformed after he grew afraid of his heavy responsibilities. Finding the courage to reach him, she embraces him, restoring his human form, and helps him perform the ceremony, which brings the water back to the kingdom. Returning home, where only hours have passed, Akane celebrates her birthday with new self-assurance.

Critics praised the visuals but found the story uneven. Matt Schley of The Japan Times gave it three out of five stars, judging that it pushes the Miyazaki buttons successfully on the surface but lacks a deeper emotional core, and Allan Hunter of Screen Daily felt that its overly busy story plays like a string of set pieces rather than building dramatic momentum.

In the small town of Coldwater Hills, Julie is a well-liked student who works as a waitress at the local diner while she waits to leave for college. She is charmed by David, a young, dashing officer newly hired by the local police, and begins dating him, seeing the romance as a fun distraction until she moves on. David, however, takes the relationship far more seriously. Even on their first date he gives her a music box, and he soon becomes possessive, needlessly suspicious of her male co-worker and angry when she does not answer his calls, telling her that he always wants to be able to find her. As he turns from doting boyfriend into controlling ex and then dangerous stalker, Julie seeks help from the police, but to no avail: David's father was also an officer on the force and a friend of the chief, and David easily charms the townspeople, who trust him more than her. Isolated, she finds herself in a deadly game of cat and mouse, and after being tormented and left for dead by her scorned lover, she must summon the strength to recover and fight back against her abuser. The story also weaves Native American elements into its storytelling.

The film is loosely inspired by the case of Laura Kucera, a nineteen-year-old who was shot and left for dead by an ex-boyfriend in 1994. Only Mine premiered on Netflix in the United States and other countries on 15 January 2019 and returned to the platform's charts in 2021. Reviews were moderate. Heaven of Horror gave it three out of five, finding it realistic and well cast despite its Lifetime-style production, with a convincingly creepy Zimmerman. In The Independent, Clémence Michallon called it a lean, humble, clear-headed film that never romanticizes abuse and shows how it can begin with controlling behavior, praising Fauntleroy's performance, though she conceded that it is not great cinema.

Kevin, Stuart and Bob have been mailed off to Miami, but they are accidentally dropped at the North Pole instead. Spotting a light in the snow, they discover Santa's Workshop, and since it has always been their dream to meet Santa and help deliver his presents, they make the most of the situation by trying to become elves. They are not very good at it. On the toy assembly line they produce a hybrid teddy bear and train, so they are moved to gingerbread house duty. Kevin builds a beautiful gingerbread house, only for Stuart to wreck it with his gingerbread crane, while Bob manages to get himself stuck inside his own creation and Stuart starts eating the house as Kevin tries to free him. The exasperated Head Elf banishes the trio to the reindeer stables. There Bob spots a baby reindeer apparently caught in a fence post and opens the gate to help, but it is a ruse to free the reindeer from their stalls, and before long the Minions have left the whole workshop in ruins. When Santa arrives, the Minions accidentally take off with his sleigh. The short ends with the three singing a Minionese version of "Jingle Bells" over a series of photos, one of which shows them delivering presents to Who-ville, the village from The Grinch.

The short gained a wider audience on 27 November 2020, when it was broadcast on NBC as one of four mini-movies in the Minions Holiday Special, Illumination's first television special, alongside Puppy, Training Wheels and Minion Scouts.

People believe they have Camille figured out: a beautiful, spoiled daddy's girl living off her wealthy father's fortune. In reality she has fought hard to build a life free of his control. Out on her own she has made mistakes, including one that led to a stint in rehab and plenty of bad press, and she has worked her way back to independence and happiness. Now her life is threatened as a result of her father's ruthless business dealings. Caught between resentment and fear, she expects her father, a powerful tycoon, to take drastic measures to protect her, but is not prepared for the man he hires to do the job. Jake is haunted by his past: he was once distracted from duty, with devastating personal and professional consequences, and he vowed never to let it happen again. Taking on the job of bodyguard to Camille is exactly the kind of distraction he should avoid, but he soon discovers that she is not the woman the world perceives, finding her warm and compassionate, and his duty to protect her deepens into something more than a well-paid assignment, even as he believes he cannot have both the absolution he seeks and Camille. The romance develops alongside the mystery of the threats, and the eventual revelation of who is behind them involves blackmail of her father over compromising photographs.

Reactions were mixed. A reviewer for The Guide to Romance, a devoted fan of the novel, felt Passionflix had brought the book to life, praising the accents, scenery, smooth transitions and music and recommending it, while finding the chemistry between the leads weaker than expected. The PolyBlog was negative, describing a made-for-television feel with low-budget action and schmaltzy romance, awkward flashbacks and a villain's plan that made no sense, and criticizing much of the acting, though it found Rigby decent to watch.

Quinn pulls himself out of a park fountain in Ho Chi Minh City, soaking wet and with no clear memory of who he is, only fragmented visions of a rotting labyrinth, cloaked figures who can bend reality and his missing daughter Lucy. He discovers that three days earlier, by his own reckoning, he was in England in 1985, but it is now 2018. Struggling to speak through a severe stammer, he wanders the city and is pursued by mysterious figures. Meanwhile Connor, a former military man working as an assassin for a local Chinese gang boss, wakes to find his wife gone; dismissing what seemed a dream of aliens taking her, he blames a rival gang and goes on the warpath. The psychiatrist Dr. Pham, who treats Quinn, brings the two men together, and they learn that an invisible alien race stationed above the fountain is abducting people with especially strong qi, the life force it needs to return home. The drones serving the aliens can only be stopped by pulling a small robotic spider from their necks. Together the trio set out to rescue the abducted and stop a portal to the aliens' world from opening.

The Blu-ray release included both a director's cut and a producer's cut. Reviews were mixed to positive. Justin Harrison of Birth.Movies.Death. called it shaky but enjoyable, praising Adkins for playing against type as a vulnerable, disoriented hero and the film's eerie atmosphere, while faulting its blunt exposition and familiar characters. Paul Bramhall of City on Fire rated it 7 out of 10, enjoying its goofy premise, Adkins's rare comedic turn, his reunion with On and the fight choreography.

Described by HBO as revealing "the tears and triumphs involved in the challenge of bringing the fantasy world of Westeros to life" in the studios, fields and car parks of Northern Ireland, the documentary mixes behind-the-scenes footage with interviews. Rather than concentrating only on the stars and writers, it gives equal attention to production assistants, costume designers, set decorators, caterers and carpenters, revealing the scale of the effort behind the production. It opens with the cast's first reading of the final scripts and closes with the wrap of filming.

HBO approached Finlay, a casual fan of the series, after being impressed by her earlier documentaries such as The Great Hip Hop Hoax (2013) and Orion (2015). After meeting with producers David Benioff, D. B. Weiss, Bernadette Caulfield and Carolyn Strauss, she was given full autonomy and unrestricted access to the set, alternating weeks on the production with work on her documentary Seahorse. The project was kept secret from all but those directly involved, and Finlay received the season's scripts before some of the cast had read them so that she could decide whose reactions to film at the table read. Composer Hannah Peel was commissioned to write the score in late 2017. Filming wrapped alongside the season in July 2018, with more than 950 hours of footage shot over 14 months, and Finlay delivered her final cut two weeks before the season premiered.

Beyoncé had originally been booked to headline Coachella in April 2017 but postponed because of her pregnancy with twins. Playing the rescheduled dates on 14 and 21 April 2018, she became the first Black woman to headline the festival, performing a 26-song set before some 125,000 concertgoers in a show quickly nicknamed "Beychella". The film interweaves footage of both weekends, with their ensemble of dancers and guest appearances by her Destiny's Child bandmates Kelly Rowland and Michelle Williams, her husband Jay-Z and her sister Solange, with behind-the-scenes footage of rehearsals and glimpses of her life, including her pregnancy and her return to performing after giving birth. The show itself pays tribute to the culture of historically black colleges, with a full marching band, majorette dancers, a step show and strolling pledges echoing Black Greek life, and opens with her singing "Lift Every Voice and Sing", often called the Black national anthem. Drawing on Black feminism, it samples Black writers and thinkers such as Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie and Malcolm X. Her mother Tina Knowles recalled worrying that Coachella's largely white audience might not understand a show so steeped in Black culture, to which Beyoncé replied that her platform gave her a responsibility to do what was best for the world rather than what was most popular.

Homecoming received near-universal acclaim, and was widely described as one of the greatest concert films ever made; The Washington Post's Chris Richards called it exactly that, and The Atlantic's Spencer Kornhaber considered it a career-defining document. Nielsen reported that it drew more than a million US viewers on its first day. It won the Grammy Award for Best Music Film and Best Music Documentary at the IDA Documentary Awards, and received six Primetime Emmy nominations.

The short fills in what happened to Bo Peep between Toy Story 2 and Toy Story 4. After reuniting with Woody, Bo, joined by her friend Giggle, tells him in a series of flashbacks how she became a lost toy. Once part of a nursery lamp in the bedroom of Andy's younger sister Molly, Bo and her sheep were given away when Molly outgrew them. In her next home, a child's bedroom, she is bored because the mother will not let the children play with the lamp, and as the years pass she moves through a montage of temporary homes, including a white elephant party where teenagers treat her roughly, at one point setting her on fire. She eventually lands in the Second Chance Antiques store, where she is safe but bored once again, and where Gabby Gabby and her ventriloquist dummies make a brief appearance. Wanting adventure and the chance to be played with, Bo devises a plan with Giggle, outwits the shop's surprisingly elaborate security system and breaks out with her sheep, beginning a free life as a lost toy.

LaPointe built the short partly from flashback material cut from Toy Story 4, which had been sad in tone, reworking the gags into comedy as Bo looks back on her hard life with humor. She received guidance from Pete Docter and producer Jonas Rivera, and kept the lamp at the center of the frame while cutting through time, seasons and settings. Lamp Life premiered on Disney+ on 31 January 2020. Reviewers found it charming and packed with quick gags and Pixar Easter eggs, though Laughing Place considered it a tame series of vignettes that added little to the character.

The story opens with Sasha, a sixteen-year-old who wants to impress his friends and posts a doctored picture of himself with an attractive girl in a group chat. Seven years later he is a successful young man living in Moscow and preparing to marry his beloved fiancée Katya. Their contentment is disturbed when Sasha receives a message from the same girl asking to meet him, while Katya begins to suffer terrifying visions of a female ghost. Katya learns that the girl, Masha, with whom Sasha had once corresponded online, recently killed her own former fiancé in a bloody attack and then took her own life. Believing that a church wedding will protect them, the couple marry quickly, but the ceremony fails to stop the spirit, which goes on killing anyone who gets in its way. Guided by a priest fighting to save Sasha's life, Katya must arrange a funeral service for Masha, whose body has still not been buried and whose soul has been seized by a demonic force.

Konstantin Beloshapka plays Sasha and Vera Kincheva plays Katya, with Zhanna Danilova as Masha, Elena Morozova as Masha's mother, Sergey Dvoynikov and Yekaterina Shumakova as the couple's friends Oleg and Zhenya, and Vladimir Seleznyov as the priest, Father Aleksei.

Made on a reported budget of about 50 million rubles, the film earned roughly 290,000 US dollars in Russia. Reviewing it for Kinoafisha, Asya Zabolotskaya called it a stereotypical horror film in a Russian setting that borrows the style of American B-movies. She felt the horror atmosphere worked reasonably well and that the cast approached the material with real affection, and she noted the sepia-tinted look of locations such as an empty hospital. However, she found the suspense built on familiar devices like jarring music, sudden blackouts and slow camera moves, criticised the uneven, television-style dramaturgy, and suggested the plot would be forgotten soon after viewing.

The film opens as Meghan shoots her final wedding scene on the legal drama Suits before moving to London, where Harry welcomes her to Kensington Palace with a homemade banner and champagne. As the wedding approaches, she struggles with royal protocol and a hostile press, embodied by a fictional morning show, Good Day UK, and its racist co-host. She attends her first royal Christmas, plans the guest list, supports victims of the Grenfell Tower fire and argues with palace staff over her white gown and tiara. When her father, Thomas Markle, is exposed for staging paparazzi photographs and then withdraws from the ceremony, Charles and Camilla reassure her, and Charles offers to escort her for part of the walk down the aisle. After the wedding the duchess promotes a charity cookbook created with women from a community kitchen formed after the fire, realizes she is pregnant as Harry gives her a puppy, and decides she will no longer suppress her own style, discarding the pantyhose palace aides expect her to wear. The film ends with a real photograph of the couple holding their newborn baby.

Lifetime announced the project in February 2019, and the film premiered on Memorial Day, 27 May 2019. It was followed by Harry & Meghan: Escaping the Palace. Reception was divided. Newsweek reported that viewers were split over the new cast and the gossip-driven plot, though Entertainment Tonight's Philiana Ng praised Smith's performance. Vanity Fair's Julie Miller described it as a budget-conscious attempt to theorize about what happened behind palace doors, and a recap by Martha Sorren and Lia Beck complained that the film skipped the wedding itself in favor of the cookbook storyline.

Taiwanese actor Darren Wang plays Sang Yu, a struggling, impoverished screenwriter whose scripts have never been filmed. Crippled by writer's block and months of insomnia, he cannot deliver the screenplay demanded by his producer San Ge (Cao Bingkun), and every time he does fall asleep a demonic blue creature hunts him down and kills him in his dreams. After losing his apartment and ending up on the streets, Sang reaches the point of attempting suicide, but a street pancake vendor stops him and advises him to remind himself, during his next nightmare, that he is only dreaming so that he can wake up before dying. Following this advice, Sang wakes to find himself holding the golden sword that had just wounded him in the dream. The priceless object fetches a fortune, and by repeating the trick night after night he collects valuable artefacts from the dream world and becomes rich almost overnight. San Ge now becomes his subordinate, and Sang finally finds the courage to court Hua Er (Song Jia), the café owner he has long admired from afar. His wealth carries a cost, however: injuries from the dream world keep following him into reality, and his money draws the attention of a ruthless gangster boss, Qiang (Wu Gang). King Shih-chieh and Kevin Lee also appear.

Critical responses varied. Writing for Yahoo News Singapore, Teng Yong Ping gave it three out of five stars, reading it as a fable warning against unearned wealth; he found its effects decent but below Hollywood level and faulted Wang's broad acting, the vague rules of the dream world and an anti-climactic ending. M.N. Miller of Ready Steady Cut was far more enthusiastic, calling it great fun and interpreting the dream demon as a metaphor for a writer's inner struggles. AsianMovieWeb judged it surprisingly entertaining as a fantasy comedy with a subtle romance and neat effects, though it felt the script grew too convoluted towards the end.

The Survivor is a 2021 biographical drama directed by Barry Levinson from a screenplay by Justine Juel Gillmer, based on Alan Scott Haft's book about his father, the boxer Harry Haft. Ben Foster stars as Haft, with Vicky Krieps, Billy Magnussen, Peter Sarsgaard, John Leguizamo, Danny DeVito and Dar Zuzovsky. It was produced by New Mandate Films, Bron Studios and Creative Wealth Media, with a score by Hans Zimmer.

The story moves between the Holocaust and its aftermath. At Auschwitz, the young Polish Jew Harry survives because the SS officer Dietrich Schneider (Magnussen), after seeing him strike another officer, decides to turn him into a fighter, staging bouts against fellow prisoners for the entertainment and wagers of the camp's officers; winning means food, losing means death. In 1949, Harry is a struggling heavyweight in the United States, still haunted by guilt and obsessed with finding Leah (Zuzovsky), the love he lost before the war. He hopes that a high-profile fight against the rising star Rocky Marciano will make him famous enough for her to find him. He confides his wartime story to the reporter Emory Anderson (Sarsgaard), but when the article is published, members of the Jewish community condemn him as a traitor. Marciano's trainer Charlie Goldman (DeVito) offers him a few days of training at a camp upstate, alongside his trainer Pepe (Leguizamo), so that he will not be destroyed in the ring. Miriam Wofsoniker (Krieps), who works for an agency helping survivors find lost relatives, assists in his search and gradually becomes part of his new life, while memories of the camp, triggered by everyday moments such as fireworks, keep intruding. Harry ultimately loses to Marciano but begins to come to terms with the past.

In 2020, Mamoru Suzuhara (Kitamura) is a bookish, solitary high-school second-year in the old mining town of Satomiya, steeped in military history. Shortly before the summer holidays he learns that his childhood friend and neighbour Aya Chiyono (Yoshine), whom he has long loved, is about to move to Tokyo, because her father, a local politician, plans to run for a Tokyo seat. Aya, who wanted at least to spend her birthday a week later in her hometown, accepts Mamoru's proposal to run away, and dressing it up as a "camp", she invites classmates until six of them are living in a disused mine on a hill. There they find Malet, a Thai child hiding from immigration officers after being separated from her parents. When officials arrive and lock the teenagers in, Mamoru shields Malet and the six are drawn into a seven-day "war" against the adults. Following Mamoru's tactics, they thwart a search, and post videos of their stand online to draw onlookers. Aya's father, his secretary and a construction company run by the father of Aya's best friend Kaori try to break in, and when the secretary exposes the group's old secrets on social media, tensions erupt. Eventually each confesses the feelings they had kept hidden, including Aya, who reveals that she is gay, and the reunited friends launch a final plan to save Malet.

The film opened in Japan on 13 December 2019 and was selected for the feature competition at the 2020 Annecy festival. It won the award for best animated feature at the Sitges Film Festival, and in France, where Eurozoom released it as 7 Jours in 2021, Télérama called it a successful adaptation of a classic of Japanese youth literature, while Le Monde found its themes too numerous.

Lucas is a reserved young man who lives with his charitable, deeply religious Aunt Lourdes in a quiet country town. He helps her by playing hymns on his keyboard at the religious meetings she holds in the living room with the local ladies, and he gives music lessons to an eccentric young woman whose increasingly inappropriate advances he has to fend off. His tranquil routine is upended when Lourdes announces the arrival of another nephew he barely knows, Mario, a distant cousin who has just spent a couple of weeks in jail over a mix-up and cannot return home because his abusive father has rejected him. Shortly before Mario arrives for what is meant to be a brief stay, Lourdes leaves on a trip, so the two young men are left alone and Lucas must share his bedroom with the newcomer. The contrast between the uninhibited, scrappy ex-prisoner and his repressed, closeted cousin produces comic situations, while playful flirting gradually builds into sexual tension and then a passionate romance. The story also mocks the hypocrisy of the town's devout churchgoers and homophobes, and the aunt turns out to have a few surprises of her own.

Cazado said he wanted to make a love story that defied moral standards but in a light way, something fun with a happy ending that would encourage audiences to believe they could love whom they want and be accepted by their families. The film was released in Brazil in 2019 and distributed on home video and on demand in the United Kingdom by TLA Releasing from December 2019. English-language reviewers were generally warm. Culture Fix praised the charming central performances, the uplifting tone and a satire of judgmental religion it likened to John Waters, while Derek Winnert gave it four stars, calling it sweet and good-natured and highlighting the chemistry between Cazado and Sousa as well as Zancanaro's performance as the drinking, smoking, swearing aunt. Some Brazilian critics, including Cinema com Rapadura, were harsher, describing it as a weak fable about overcoming prejudice.

Kento Yamazaki plays Nagata, a struggling playwright and director who co-founded the small theatre company Oroka with his school friend Nohara (Kanichiro Sato). His avant-garde productions draw poor reviews and few ticket sales, and his relations with the troupe are deteriorating. Wandering the streets in a daze, he stops at a gallery window and notices a young woman, Saki (Mayu Matsuoka), who is wearing the same sneakers as him. Saki has come to Tokyo from Aomori to study at a fashion college and dreams of becoming an actress, and the two fall in love. Nagata soon moves into her apartment, contributing nothing towards the rent while she works several jobs. Over the years his insecurity, jealousy of other people's success and possessive, dismissive treatment of her gradually wear Saki down, leaving her depressed and drinking heavily as she nears thirty. A former troupe member, Aoyama (Sairi Ito), and Nohara confront him about his behaviour, and Nagata ultimately turns their story into a stage play. Satoru Iguchi of the band King Gnu appears as Komine, a rival playwright of the same age, with Shusaku Kamikawa, Ritsu Otomo and Kodai Asaka in supporting roles.

The film, made by The Fool and distributed by Shochiku and Aniplex, was due to open on 17 April 2020, but the release was postponed indefinitely as COVID-19 spread in Japan. In June, Yoshimoto Kogyo took over distribution, and the film opened in cinemas on 17 July 2020 while also streaming worldwide on Amazon Prime Video the same day, reportedly the first time a Japanese live-action feature had done so.

Sairi Ito won the Blue Ribbon Award for Best Supporting Actress. Reviews were divided over the central character. The Japan Times headlined its review as a tortured romance with no sparks, while Windows on Worlds read the film as a portrait of toxic narcissism and abusive behaviour, seen only through Nagata's eyes, that ends with him rediscovering his love of theatre and accepting that a chapter of life has closed.

Within a matter of weeks, a massive surge of glacial melting plunges the Northern Hemisphere into a new ice age. Glaciers devastate cities such as New York and Paris, the Eiffel Tower collapses and even the pyramids of Giza are buried in snow. In the United States, Mark (Joel Berti) and his wife Helen (Jennifer Lee Wiggins), a scientist, are forced to flee the cold. Their weather-obsessed daughter Brie (Lauren Esposito) and her boyfriend Tyler (Charles Townsend) are out studying the phenomenon when Tyler loses control of their car, and they escape just before it plunges into a chasm. Chased by a pack of wolves, they shelter in a school, where they join a group of students led by Aliyah (Anna Christensen) and Roger (Blake Dang). After an avalanche buries the entrance, the group barricades itself against the weather and the wolves, and Roger finds a pistol and propane tanks in the janitor's office.

Mark and Helen set out to find their daughter, parting from their colleague Larry (Erickson), who heads alone for a military post. Helen squeezes into the iced-over school, evades a wolf and reunites with Brie and Tyler, who are now engaged. Roger blows open the blocked entrance by shooting the propane tanks. While the students drive towards the military station, the family makes for a research station on a nearby plateau where the weather has inexplicably stayed normal, hoping to understand why and share the findings with the world. On the way they lose their car and are confronted by a gang of looters who want Mark's bag of research instruments; lightning from a freezing storm kills most of them, and Helen knocks out the surviving leader before the family finds another vehicle and reaches the plateau.

German critics were dismissive. The German film magazine Filmdienst described it as a low-budget variation on blockbuster disaster scenarios, told with deadly seriousness, with miserable effects and characters left undeveloped, while Cinema dismissed it as Ice Age without the gags or cute animals.

Emily, who has never worked as a carer before, is driven by her employer to her new job as the night carer for Arthur, a bedridden elderly man with dementia who is barely ever conscious. Before she starts, the day carer asks the employer whether they should tell her something, but he insists there is nothing to tell. He gives Emily a brief tour of the old house, showing her the camera and monitor and mentioning an upstairs that no one uses any more, and then leaves her alone for the long night. Almost at once strange things begin to happen. She gets locked out of the house, doors creak open and slam shut, objects turn up in different places, Arthur claims that someone is standing behind her, and she thinks she glimpses a figure. With no electricity in most rooms, she explores by flashlight, finding furniture under dust sheets and a girl's bedroom still full of belongings. In a bag apparently left behind by the previous carer she discovers tools for communicating with the dead, including a Ouija board, along with charms meant to ward off harmful spirits. Using the board, Emily makes contact with a vengeful presence and, as the night grows more terrifying, uncovers the house's dark secrets, before a final twist recasts what has come before.

The film was an official selection of the Screamfest horror festival in Los Angeles in 2018, and was released on video on demand in the United States in May 2020 before arriving on Hulu that September. Reviews were largely negative. Brandon of PopHorror credited Stevens's performance with keeping the film alive and admired its sparse, realistic chills, while finding the plot thin and the twist confusing. Cynthia Vinney of CBR called it all atmosphere and no substance, criticizing its lack of momentum, grimy look, reliance on the score and a twist that made no sense. John Serba of Decider likewise recommended skipping it, describing it as almost entirely a woman walking slowly through a house.

Kristine Kujath Thorp stars as Sofia, a young researcher working on an underwater search drone, who lives with oil worker Stian (Henrik Bjelland) and his young son Odin (Nils Elias Olsen). When a platform suddenly sinks, Sofia and her colleague Arthur (Rolf Kristian Larsen) are sent to the site, where their drone finds bodies and a lone survivor trapped in an air pocket. Before he can be rescued, gas bursts from a crack in the seabed and a violent explosion destroys the platform, wounding Sofia. Reviewing the footage, Arthur discovers that the official explanation is wrong: a gigantic fault is opening on the floor of the North Sea, threatening every installation in the area and a catastrophic oil spill. The operator begins an emergency evacuation and orders all wells sealed, but on Stian's platform one valve fails to close automatically, and he volunteers to shut it by hand. The last helicopter leaves without him and he is presumed dead. Refusing to accept this, Sofia studies the surveillance footage, concludes he may have survived, and flies out to the stricken platform unofficially with Arthur to find him, just as the authorities decide to ignite the spreading slick from the air. Anders Baasmo Christiansen, Bjørn Floberg and Anneke von der Lippe play key roles.

Rather than relying chiefly on spectacle, the film devotes much of its attention to how the Norwegian authorities handle the crisis. It received seven nominations at the 2022 Amanda Awards, Norway's national film prizes, including Best Norwegian Film, and won the award for Best Visual Effects. Writing for Film.ru, Konstantin Myshkin gave it seven out of ten, observing that the oppressive mood Andersen creates lingers past the end credits, since the individual characters may be saved but humanity's relationship with nature seemingly cannot.

The story is framed as Samuel's account of how he met Floyd, a memoir that later becomes a literary sensation. At his lowest point, a despondent Samuel leaves his apartment, rides a bus out of town and wanders the streets until he is struck by a Cadillac driven by Floyd, an enigmatic, middle-aged father of two who was eating ice cream at the wheel. Mortified at having badly injured him, Floyd visits him in the hospital and offers a deal: free room and board in his large suburban home and 500 dollars in cash a week if Samuel will write his biography. Samuel moves in with the eccentric Deveraux family, which includes Jacqueline, who at one point attempts to seduce him, the tween Edward, a death metal fan with disturbing interests, and the teenage Lily, a former violin prodigy who walked away from her career by smashing her instrument at a recital. As he listens to Floyd's tall tales, Samuel is plagued by vivid nightmares and hallucinations, including a talking Santa doll in his room, and the line between reality and delusion blurs, especially after the menacing, inhaler-using Anselm draws him and Floyd into violent trouble.

In a fantasy world where adventurers take contracts from the Guild, the nameless Goblin Slayer is a silver-ranked warrior devoted solely to exterminating goblins, having survived as a child the goblin raid that destroyed his village. The Sword Maiden asks him and his party to travel to the snowy mountains of the north to learn what became of the Noble Fencer, a young noblewoman whose party of novice adventurers vanished after setting out to hunt goblins. Along the way they find a small village under attack and a mysterious chapel, and Goblin Slayer is troubled by the unusual way these goblins behave. They rescue the Noble Fencer, who has survived horrific abuse at the hands of her captors but refuses to abandon the fight, determined to recover the sword they stole from her and take revenge. The trail leads to an ancient fortress buried in snow, which the goblins defend like an army, and there the party must face a goblin leader able to wield magic, an ability previously believed to belong only to the human-like races. The Noble Fencer finds strength in her bond with Priestess and High Elf Archer as the battle unfolds.

Goblin's Crown premiered in Japanese theaters on 1 February 2020 and was licensed by Crunchyroll. Its main story runs about an hour, preceded by a recap of the television series. Reviews were mostly unfavorable. Kim Morrissy of Anime News Network gave it a D, arguing that condensing an entire novel into roughly sixty minutes left its emotional moments without weight and made the Noble Fencer's recovery abrupt; she also criticized the goblins' convenient intelligence, the stilted animation and the decision to make the creatures increasingly human-like, though she praised the music and ending theme. Other reviewers enjoyed the snowy setting and the action but also noted the long recap and rushed character development.

Zhenya (Enzhaeva), a dressmaker, is devastated when she finds her boyfriend Kir (Beloshapka), an artist and the father of their baby daughter Polina, having sex with one of his models, and he pushes her away. Told that only a love spell can bring him back, she visits a Romani fortune-teller, Aza (Akhmedova), who instructs her to perform a ritual during the wedding of someone she knows. Zhenya chooses the wedding of her client Sonya (Borodina) and the doctor Viktor (Ermolov), and hides on the church balcony during the service to carry out the rite with candles and scraps of cloth, even eating raw meat. Afterwards she collapses on the church steps and is rushed to Viktor's hospital, while Viktor soon finds his new wife with another man, though Sonya protests she does not know what came over her. Kir does return to Zhenya, but his renewed love turns into frightening obsession and jealousy: he attacks her friends, chases her in a car, tries to encase her body in plaster and cuts off his own mother's finger at the dinner table to take a family ring for his proposal. Even after Kir's death the spell keeps its hold, turning Zhenya's life into a nightmare as his spirit pursues anyone standing between him and his beloved, and at one point she is trapped in a mortuary cabinet with his corpse. The story culminates in a ceremony in the church to break the spell.

Reviews were mixed. Gulnaz Davletshina of Kinoafisha praised its dramatic exploration of how an exhausted relationship can drive someone into a dark corner but felt the idea was underdeveloped, with too many demons and too little humanity. Moria awarded it three stars for heading into pleasingly dark places, while Brian Orndorf found it bland and lacking real menace.

Van, once the leader of the Dokkaku, a fabled band of warriors, has been defeated by the mighty Tsuol Empire and enslaved in a salt mine. One night a pack of strange wild dogs attacks the mine, spreading a deadly illness known as Black Wolf Fever. Everyone dies except Van, who survives despite being bitten, and Yuna, a little girl he rescues. The pair escape and find refuge in the countryside, where Van comes to love Yuna like a daughter. The plague, however, has been deliberately unleashed by the king of Akafa, a vassal state that hopes to weaken the empire and regain its power.

Hossal, a brilliant physician of the empire, deduces that Van carries antibodies to the disease and sets out to find him in order to make a cure from his blood, while the assassin Sae is sent to hunt him down. The dogs are controlled by Kenoi, an aging man known as the King of Dogs, who has Yuna abducted to force Van to become his successor. Van follows her to a hidden village where survivors of Akafa, led by the warrior Ohfan, plot a rebellion against the Tsuol emperor with the help of the dogs. Hossal reaches the village and succeeds in making a serum from Van's blood. Van refuses Kenoi's legacy, but Yuna shares the same power and, in a trance, leads the pack toward the emperor. Van stops her just in time, breaks the spell and departs alone with the dogs, choosing to become their king so that Yuna can live in peace. Hossal uncovers why the people of Akafa had been protected from the fever, the rebellion is abandoned, and years later the grown Yuna glimpses the Deer King leading the pack in the mountains.

The film competed at the Annecy International Animation Film Festival in June 2021. Its Japanese release, delayed twice by the COVID-19 pandemic, finally took place on 4 February 2022 through Toho.

Kanata Morita (Miyoshi) is a young psychologist who is able to perceive the dead. Her brother Yuma (Bando) and his girlfriend Akina (Otani) go looking for the legendary village, said to lie beyond an abandoned tunnel and to be reachable only after answering a phone that rings at 2 a.m. in a lonely booth by a bridge. Their visit is cut short by shadowy figures. Back home Akina behaves strangely and falls to her death from a tower, yet her autopsy shows that she drowned. When Yuma and their younger brother Kota then disappear while searching for answers, and people around the family begin dying in bizarre circumstances, Kanata travels to the sealed tunnel herself. Her investigation leads her into the village's buried past, including its flooding for a dam, and reveals that her own family and bloodline are bound up with its curse and its former residents, forcing her to confront the truth about her ancestors and herself.

The children's song "Futashicharo" heard in the film was written by Shimizu rather than drawn from the legend. A preview screening was held in Miyawaka, the Fukuoka city where the tunnel lies, and a version that softened the scares with cute dog animation and comic sound effects was later released for viewers averse to horror. The film won the jury prize at the 2020 Gérardmer Fantastic Film Festival. Critics found it atmospheric but overstuffed: Horror News Net praised its mix of folklore and urban legend, while Heaven of Horror gave it three out of five, citing confusing, unresolved plot threads but a strong performance by Miyoshi.

The year is 463 AD. Arthur has spent five years abroad fighting the Roman Empire, drinking heavily and picking fights, and has lost both Excalibur and his faith in his own ability to rule. During his absence his illegitimate son Mordred has seized power in Camelot. Caring little for his father's legacy, the bitter young man is purging or imprisoning those who oppose him, including Queen Guinevere, colluding with a witch, plotting a deal with the invading Saxons and planning to marry the queen against her will to legitimize his claim to the throne. Arthur returns to Britain, and flashbacks fill in past events, including how he and his old friend Lancelot first found Guinevere. Reluctant to resume his responsibilities, the king must wrestle with the question of whether he is truly the right man to lead, gather his rag-tag band of knights of the Round Table and reclaim Excalibur before he can hope to retake his crown. Mordred's witch seems to be sapping his will and picking off members of his band in the dangerous woods, while Merlin, who has not lost faith in Arthur's destiny, challenges him to live up to the legend.

Alderson shot the film using only natural light, with large numbers of candles for the interior scenes, letting rain, mud and grey skies set the tone in its woodland locations. Critics were unimpressed. Jennie Kermode of Eye for Film found that it acquitted itself better than some entries in the genre because it had an idea of its own and maintained its grittiness, but judged it padded and overlong, with a two-dimensional Mordred and little for the female characters to do. Dan Jolin of Empire called it a forgettable fantasy cheapie with a thin, muddled story, a strained lead performance and a title character who appears in only two scenes.

The title refers to Israel's Law of Return, which grants citizenship to Jews from anywhere in the world. Under it, Major Ronan Jackson (Sawa), an American-trained F-16 pilot whose mother was Jewish, has emigrated and flies for the Israeli Air Force. Jackson is also the son of a United States senator (Patrick). After a mission he is shot down over Syria and, having survived the crash, becomes the target of an Iranian-backed militia led by a shadowy and ruthless commander known as the Ghost. Because of who his father is, Washington and Jerusalem agree on a joint operation that officially does not exist: a squad of Marines under Gunnery Sergeant Dave Torres (Nolasco) is teamed with a unit of Israeli commandos and a Mossad agent (Eitan) and sent behind enemy lines to bring Jackson out within 36 hours. While the two teams trade barbs and learn to work together, and a Marine general (Cross) argues the case at headquarters, Jackson evades his pursuers alone, armed only with a pistol, hiding in fields and trying to keep his identity from being discovered. The rescue turns into a running series of firefights that ends in sacrifice for members of the squad.

Reviews were largely negative. Roger Moore of Movie Nation found the firefights routine and the details sloppy, mocking a sequence in which militiamen fire over the sunflowers where Jackson is hiding, and judged the film gory and trigger-happy but cut-rate and unsatisfying, with a tone he likened to propaganda. Darren Lucas of Movies Reviews 101 considered it watchable and noted good chemistry within the squad, but felt it brought nothing new to the rescue-mission genre and offered no truly engaging characters, while also criticising its shaky-camera action.

Claire is a hard-working nurse at a busy local hospital who truly cares about her patients. Her life at work is made miserable by her supervisor, who lingers at the nurses' station, avoids taking care of patients herself and loads Claire with tedious extra tasks, aided by other "mean girl" nurses who try to make her look bad to the bosses. Her only relief is the patients she treats, and even that is not always easy, since one cranky man has no interest in anything the doctors or nurses do for him. On a rare night off, Claire's roommate Lena, a ballet dancer, gives her a ticket to an evening performance, but on the way Claire becomes trapped in a malfunctioning elevator with a charming man and a waiter. They miss the entire show, spending hours talking, and feel an instant connection, but in the bustle of their rescue they are pulled apart before they can exchange names or numbers. Soon afterwards the hospital's new doctor arrives, and Claire realizes that he is Luke, the man from the elevator. Luke cannot stop thinking about the woman he met that night, yet he fails to recognize her in her nurse's scrubs and, focused on his first days in the job, is brusque with her, while the supervisor reprimands Claire for supposedly making advances towards him. When an evening event is held at the hospital and Claire is assigned to work through it, some of her grateful patients find her a dress and shoes and others volunteer to cover her shift, giving her the chance to attend.

Reviewers treated it as a light, clean, Hallmark-style romance. Rissi JC of RissiWrites found it a darling romance that evoked the Cinderella story without obvious cues, praising Murray as a good Cinderella and a hero who is far from perfect, though she felt the mean-girl subplot went overboard. Patty's 365 Films review liked it, giving it three and a half stars.

Ashley-Kae, a somewhat odd college student fascinated by history, photography and nuns, has been fixated since childhood on the legend of Sister Monday, a renegade nun once assigned to a jail who was suspected of murdering many of the prisoners in her care, following a suspicious fire that burned a church to the ground, and who vanished before she could be caught. The stories her father told her about the nun terrified her as a child, and she still carries a frightening secret from that time. She sets off for a weekend at her family's vacation cabin with her shallow, bored sister Gabby, Gabby's juvenile, beer-drinking boyfriend Anthony, and Michael, Ashley-Kae's awkward friend who hopes to be more than a friend. When they stop so that Ashley-Kae can photograph an old church, Anthony's car keys go missing, and with no phone signal and a rainstorm rolling in, the group is forced to take shelter for the night in the abandoned jail where Sister Monday once held court. As the four wait out the storm, bickering and joking, the vengeful spirit of the nun begins to pick them off one by one, and the story builds towards a twist.

Reviews were generally favorable. Stuart D. Monroe of Horror DNA found that it subverted the expectations of nunsploitation by avoiding gratuitous blasphemy and nudity, praising its clean, polished look, the chemistry of the cast, Willis's endearing performance and Rose's stern, understated menace, along with a bold turn in its story, though he wished the backstory of the church fire had been developed further. Morbidly Beautiful rated it 3.5 out of 5, calling it a fun, often funny midnight horror film with a creepy atmosphere and bloody deaths that showcased Rose, while noting that its talky middle section lagged.

Sharon Elliott (Klebe) runs her own real estate business and is raising her teenage son Anthony (Cabanas) alone after the mysterious murder of her husband Mark (King). Since his father's death Anthony has withdrawn from her and become socially isolated, struggling to fit in at school. Sharon is relieved and grateful when Dylan Warren (Buchanan), one of the most popular boys at the school, befriends Anthony and becomes a steadying presence for him. Dylan also becomes a sympathetic listener for Sharon herself, who confides in him about her conflicting feelings toward her late husband: Anthony grieves an idealised version of his father, while Sharon remembers Mark as a self-centred man who was hard to be married to. As Dylan spends more and more time at the house, Sharon begins to suspect that his interest lies with her rather than with her son. She does not realise that she and Dylan are bound by a dark connection from her past, or that his friendship with Anthony is part of a scheme of revenge against her, and she must uncover the truth before it destroys the family she has left.

Writing for Vocal, one Lifetime reviewer saw the film as a variation on one of the channel's most familiar premises, a vulnerable woman letting a secretly dangerous man into her life, but rated it highly for its well-developed characters, the emotionally charged scenes between mother and son, and an ending that avoids the usual Lifetime conventions in favour of a more realistic note. The review singled out Klebe's performance as well as the subtle menace and believable charm Buchanan brings to Dylan. Viewer reactions on IMDb were more divided, with several criticising the script and the supporting performances.

In a version of Paris where people with superpowers are part of everyday life, Lieutenant Gary Moreau (Marmaï), once the police liaison to the disbanded hero team the Royal Pack, investigates super-crimes. Paired with Cécile Schaltzmann (Pons), a newcomer from the financial brigade, he looks into a wave of incidents caused by a drug that grants temporary powers to ordinary people, such as a bullied teenager who takes revenge using fire. Moreau's friend Monte Carlo (Poelvoorde), a retired Royal Pack hero living with Parkinson's disease, points him toward an old villain, who turns out to have been killed and drained of blood to make the drug. Moreau also notices Lily (Souchaud), a schoolgirl whose electrical powers are just emerging.

The trail leads to Naja (Arlaud), the leader of a gang that kidnaps people with powers and turns their blood into narcotics. After the gang frees one of its dealers from a police station, it abducts Lily and her mother. Callista (Bekhti), a former Royal Pack heroine with precognitive visions who now runs a rehab program, reluctantly joins the investigation after two of her young patients die of overdoses. Moreau, who has hidden his own telekinetic powers for years, is captured and shot but survives. His friends then reveal his secret: while using his powers on a mission, he accidentally caused the explosion that killed Gigaman, Lily's father, and the guilt led him to give them up. Tracing Naja to a disgraced psychiatrist who once erased his childhood mind-control powers, the team storms his hideout. Moreau defeats the overdosing Naja and rescues Lily, and he emerges as a new hero, nicknamed Titan.

First announced at Comic Con Paris in 2015, the film closed the 2020 Deauville American Film Festival. It was subsequently sold to Netflix, which released it worldwide on 9 July 2021. Reviews were mixed: critics praised Poelvoorde's comic turn and some fresh ideas but felt the premise was underdeveloped.

Shun is a gay novelist who has settled on a small island in Okinawa after being cut off by his family in Hokkaido when they learned of his sexuality. There he meets Mio, a high school student who has lost his mother and lives with relatives. When Shun reaches out to him, the boy's prickly reaction stirs painful memories of Shun's estrangement from his parents, yet the two gradually become close. Before anything can develop, Mio reveals that he must move away to the city, promising to keep in touch.

Three years later Mio, now an adult, suddenly returns to the island and declares that he is in love with Shun. Shun is attracted to him but holds back, wracked with guilt at the idea of depriving the younger man of a so-called normal life and doubting that Mio understands what being gay will mean. Complications arrive with Sakurako, Shun's childhood friend and former fiancée, whose arranged wedding ended when Shun came out to his parents during the ceremony and who still loves him. She comes to the island to persuade him to return to Hokkaido because his father is in poor health. Shun is determined to stay with Mio, but Mio urges him to go home and make peace with his family. Realizing that Mio's feelings are sincere and his advice is right, Shun decides to return to Hokkaido and asks Mio to go with him.

The film opened in Japanese cinemas on 11 September 2020, and Funimation began streaming it in North America and other territories in July 2021. Reviews were mixed to positive. Anime News Network gave it a B-minus, feeling that it needed more time to develop its characters, especially Mio, but offered tantalizing glimpses of a satisfying love story, while The Japan Times rated it 2.5 out of 5, arguing that the adaptation lost some of the strength of the excellent manga.

The film is inspired by the urban legend surrounding the Casona Dubois in the Santiago district of Quinta Normal, now a cultural centre, where most of it was shot. According to the legend, a French engineer and his wife who settled there in the early twentieth century turned to witchcraft to conceive a child; the baby was born deformed, the father killed it and the mother took her own life, and the house has been considered cursed ever since. Title cards at the start inform the audience of this history. The story is set in 1986, during the military dictatorship. In the middle of the night Arriagada receives an urgent call: neighbours report someone inside the old mansion, crying for help. Arriagada, who that same day has committed an atrocity of his own by beating a woman labelled a subversive to death, goes to investigate, calling for reinforcements that will take time to arrive. Once inside he cannot find his way out, and the violent spirits of the family begin to torment him, including a bloodied woman who appears and vanishes, until a final twist ties the haunting to his own guilt and to the repression of the regime. Olguín shot the film quickly as an apparent single real-time take, following Cañas through the dark, labyrinthine house lit largely by his flashlight, with only a handful of actors inside the mansion.

Olguín described the film as "a great lie to tell a great truth." Reception was mixed. Patricia Reyes of La Tercera highlighted its sound design and its blend of the political context with horror, and Edgardo Viereck Salinas of Cine y Literatura considered it the director's best work, a powerful portrait of guilt under Pinochet. Reid Ramsey of Cinematary praised Cañas's physically demanding performance and the practical effects but found the scares repetitive and the concept better suited to a short film.

Ashley Seever (Hill), a cheerful party planner, travels back to her hometown for the holidays, hoping to rekindle her romance with her high school sweetheart, Grant Hines (Novlan). Her plans fall apart when she discovers that Grant is now dating Bella Vega (Lusha), a famous social media influencer. Embarrassed and unwilling to admit defeat, Ashley persuades her colleague and best friend, Liam Marsh (Little), to pose as her boyfriend for the season, and the pair stage a holiday romance in front of Grant and Bella, while Ashley's parents, Sheila (Broderick) and Winston (Eve), look on. As the pretence continues through the festivities, Ashley and Liam begin to realise that their feelings for each other may be more than an act, and Ashley has to decide whether she still wants the man she came home for or the friend who has been beside her all along.

In an interview with Gas Mask Magazine ahead of the premiere, the Texas-born Helgren described the film as a fun Christmas spin on My Best Friend's Wedding, built around a sweet party planner who returns home to revive an old flame and asks her best friend to play her fake boyfriend to avoid embarrassment. He said the team was excited that Showtime had liked the film enough to make it one of its first original Christmas acquisitions.

The film received little professional critical attention. Audience reviews on IMDb were largely negative, calling the story predictable and criticising the dialogue, the leads' chemistry and a soundtrack that some found loud enough to drown out the dialogue; Colton Little's performance was among the few elements viewers singled out for praise, while one reviewer was surprised to find the veteran British actor Trevor Eve in the cast.

Clay Kincaid owns a flourishing bar in Chicago. He hates the nickname "Saint," which he earned for being too kind to stray animals and to desperate people, especially women, and he knows he is more sinner than saint where women are concerned. Behind his success lies a rough and damaged past that has left him jaded and that may yet come back to haunt him, and as a result he does not do committed relationships. Everything changes when Samantha, a rebellious heiress turned runaway who is in need of help, walks into his bar. Clay helps her slowly get back on her feet and offers her a job as a waitress. As they work side by side, he discovers that she is someone truly special, someone who might be able to warm his damaged heart and who may be exactly the person he needs in his life. The emotional climax comes when Clay finally opens up to Samantha about his troubled past.

Markos Papadatos of Digital Journal gave the film an A rating, calling it entertaining, poignant and well crafted. He praised Gregory, whose years on the daytime drama One Life to Live he felt had paid off, for a bold, raw and vulnerable performance, singling out a gut-wrenching, monologue-heavy scene in which Clay reveals his past, described Price as sensational and credited Musk for her work as director, co-writer and showrunner. He also noted the film's emphasis on responsibility, morality and helping others in a time of need.

Loretta (Kwiatkowski), Gerry (Chambers), Danny (Naylor) and Amy (Frank) are brilliant university students attempting to prove the existence of parallel universes through a quantum physics experiment. Inspired by an aquarium in their lab, Loretta decides they need far more water and drives the group to a lake. On a winding road they come upon an accident in which another car hangs over the edge of a cliff. Loretta runs to it, apparently shocked by something, and a person inside reaches out to take her hand before Loretta plunges over the cliff with the car. Her boyfriend Danny finds comfort with Amy. Five months later, Loretta is spotted in the university library and then in a bar, and then confronts Danny and Amy, believing she is still Danny's girlfriend. When the friends explain that she vanished for five months and that they saw her die, they realise that Loretta's theory was right, a conclusion confirmed by the word "Entangled" tattooed on her forearm. It soon emerges that the other three also have tattooed doppelgängers from another reality. Amy's mother Dierdre (Matlin) immediately senses something is wrong with her daughter, and Gerry descends into madness and kills his original self so that his double can take his place. Realising that the doubles' presence is affecting their bodies the students decide to get rid of them. Returning from dumping a body in a bog along the same road, they find themselves inside the car on the cliff edge in the very accident of five months earlier, as another Loretta runs to help. The film closes as it began, with the students at the aquarium concluding that they need more water.

Multiverse received mostly negative to mixed reviews. The Lexikon des internationalen Films found its premise interesting but its plot unengaging and its emotions superficial. It was nominated for Best Canadian Feature at Whistler and for Best Film at Fantasporto 2020, and Frank and Chambers received acting nominations in Berlin.

The story takes place in winter in Forte dei Marmi, an exclusive seaside resort on the Tuscan coast that the narrator, Roberto Santini (D'Amore), likens to a picture postcard in which everything is staged. Roberto, an insomniac, runs the surveillance company whose cameras and alarms protect the town's gated villas, many of them second homes of the very rich. One night a battered young woman, Maria Spezi (Grannò), appears on the doorbell camera of a neighbouring villa pleading for help, and the frightened residents simply call security. On his way back, Roberto stops a drunk driver who turns out to be Dario (Giulio Pranno), the son of his former lover Elena (Bilello).

The carabinieri quickly blame Maria's father, Walter (Ragno), an alcoholic with a violent past who years earlier was suspected of molesting Roberto's daughter Angela (Martino) as a small child. Roberto's own footage, however, suggests that more people were involved that night, among them the industrialist Curzio Pilati (Bentivoglio), a key donor to the mayoral campaign of Roberto's wife Claudia (Sansa), and Stefano Tommasi (Muccino), a charismatic writing teacher who is sleeping with his students, Angela included. Torn between the truth, his discretion towards powerful clients and his wife's political ambitions, Roberto pursues the case as his marriage falls apart, and Dario's account finally implicates Pilati.

Filmed in Forte dei Marmi, Seravezza and Massarosa, the film premiered in Fivizzano in June 2021 and was released by Sky Italia in Italy and on Netflix elsewhere, where Chelsom said it became an unexpected hit. Reviewing it for Cineuropa, Camillo De Marco saw it less as a thriller than a psychological drama about wealthy paranoia and the troubled relationship between adults and the young, but found it short on surprises and compared it unfavorably with Human Capital, another Amidon adaptation.

The story is set in an alternate present-day America where witches are real and a constitutional amendment has stripped those with "magic in the blood" of the rights of ordinary citizens. A prologue shows a woman being burned at the stake in New England as her two red-haired daughters watch. Months later in Southern California, high school student Claire (Adlon) lives in a remote farmhouse with her widowed mother Martha (Mitchell) and her younger twin brothers. While Claire's classmates, including her friend Jen (Antariksa), mock and shun anyone suspected of being a witch, Martha secretly runs a safe house on an underground network that smuggles witches to Mexico, which still offers them asylum, and hides them in passages within the walls. The newest guests are Fiona (Cowen) and Shae (Campbell), the sisters who saw their mother executed. With agents of the federal Bureau of Witchcraft Investigation, led by the zealous Hawthorne (Camargo), closing in on anyone aiding fugitives, the sullen Claire resents the newcomers but grows fond of the calm, slightly older Fiona and begins to fear that she may have powers of her own. A reckless night out with Fiona at a local bar ends in a telekinetic outburst that threatens to expose the whole family.

Critics praised the performances but were divided on the execution. Dennis Harvey of Variety placed the film between The Craft and The Handmaid's Tale, finding its allegory about the treatment of women, minorities and immigrants fully realised but on the nose, and its action, scares and visual effects pedestrian and uneven. Shaun Munro of Flickering Myth called it a compellingly provocative spin on worn genre tropes, admiring its grounded world-building and invented lore, such as agents tracking witches with special compasses, and its evocation of historical witch trials.

The interviewees include Sarah Silverman, Adam Scott, Rosie Perez, Adam Horovitz, A$AP Rocky, Anthony Bourdain, Ben Stiller, Bill Kreutzmann, Carrie Fisher, Natasha Lyonne, Lewis Black, Nick Kroll, Reggie Watts, Shepard Fairey, Sting and Deepak Chopra, alongside Paul Scheer, Rob Corddry, Will Forte, Haley Joel Osment, Thomas Lennon and David Cross. The stories range from euphoric to frightening and absurd, and many are brought to life through animated sequences and staged re-creations. The film is among the final screen appearances of Fred Willard, Anthony Bourdain and Carrie Fisher, whose Beverly Hills home, which she called the "acid house", served as one of the locations.

Cary conceived the project in 2009 at the Nantucket Film Festival, where he, Stiller and Fisher Stevens swapped stories about hallucinogens over dinner and agreed to make a film that would combine anecdotes with re-enactments and animation. What began as a collection of funny stories grew into a work aiming to open a serious and balanced conversation about psychedelics. Over eleven years, fitting around celebrities' schedules, Cary conducted more than a hundred interviews, far more than made the final cut. The film was financed by Mike Rosenstein's Sunset Rose Pictures and Cary's Sugarshack 2000, with support from Stiller's Red Hour, and its score was provided by the indie rock band Yo La Tengo.

The film adapts the girls' final year of high school. On their class trip they begin in Nara, visiting the deer park and the Great Buddha, where Alice impresses her friends with what she knows about the sights, and continue to Kyoto, where the shy Honoka works up the nerve to ask Karen for a photo together after visiting Kinkaku-ji and Ginkaku-ji. That night Aya surprises everyone by wanting to swap stories about love, and at Kyoto Tower Shinobu and Alice talk about the future. Back home, Alice learns that her mother and Shinobu's mother met when Shinobu's mother studied in England, the reason Shinobu's homestay brought her to Alice's family. Alice struggles to tell Shinobu that she intends to return to England for her further education, and Shinobu, who has already worked it out, decides that she wants to study in England too. While Aya, Yoko and Karen prepare for Japanese entrance exams, Shinobu studies at night for overseas admission, encouraged by her family. All of them pass, and after an emotional graduation the friends part ways, until Karen, Aya and Yoko later visit Alice and Shinobu in England.

The blog The Infinite Zenith called the film a heart-warming and fitting conclusion that stays true to the series' gentle tone while letting each girl grow, and recommended it to existing fans. Other reviewers felt that compressing a large amount of manga material into the film's 82 minutes rushed the pacing and cost the story some of its relaxed atmosphere.

A prologue set in the nineteenth century introduces a wealthy hat maker whose mansion hosts decadent masquerade parties, tea, orgies and drug-fuelled excess; during one of these gatherings his young daughter accidentally starts a fire that kills everyone inside. More than a century later the "Mad Hatter", said to have been driven insane by mercury poisoning and grief, has become an urban legend. David Hart (Gutiérrez), an eccentric professor of parapsychology, recruits four college students, among them Henry (Walker), to spend a weekend in the mansion as volunteers for a study of how the supernatural affects people, telling them that the more they experience, and the more they provoke, the better. Even before the trip Henry glimpses the flickering ghost of a little girl on campus. At the house, the professor assures the group that the strange, shambling caretakers, including Berryman's character, are merely servants descended from generations of inbreeding and that the Hatter himself has long been dead. As the students start to see visions of the house's past and to disappear one by one, those who remain begin to question whether the professor's experiment is really scientific, and whether the Hatter's madness has outlived him.

Reviews were strongly negative. Harold Bleacher of Flickering Myth gave it one star, criticising the unexplained set-up, poor dialogue, thin characters, repetitive scares, flat acting, subpar computer-generated effects and a predictable twist, though he credited its musty visual scheme and underwater shots. The horror site 10th Circle rated it 2 out of 10, writing that the plot never takes off, that the characters' repeated backstories of past trauma grow tedious, and that its intrusive music and weak effects undermine any sense of horror. Other reviewers felt Berryman was underused.
